layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of formations that have become systematic: e.g. for first names in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: German (Stephanie → Steffi, Fritz → Fritzi, etc.).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hyponymy. The relation between two lexical units in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of the first is included in that of the second. E.g. any tulip

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and any rose is also a flower: therefore the words tulip and rose are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both hyponyms, and together are 'co-hyponyms', of flower.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paratactic in [[1 promised] and [he came] ].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypotaxis [haipə'taksıs]. Greek term for *subordination, applied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specifically to subordination of clauses or sentences. Opp. parataxis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('arrangement under' vs. ‘arrangement alongside') for their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *coordination. E.g. he came is hypotactic in [I said [he came]), but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothetical (conditional). See remote.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothetico-deductive method. Scientific method in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: propositions which follow from a general hypothesis are tested against

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experimental or other data to determine whether the hypothesis is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: confirmed or is false. Often applied in the 1960s and 1970s to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: validation of a *generative grammar. Thus the grammar is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothesis about the sentences of a language; from it one predicts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that certain forms are grammatical and certain others are not; if these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictions accord with the judgements of speakers the grammar is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to that extent confirmed; if not, it must in some respect be wrong.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applications.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The value of this method in linguistics is debated, in this and other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hysteron proteron. Rhetorical term from Ancient Greek for putting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: first ('proteron') what should logically be later ('hysteron’): e.g. in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recipe which says that the oven should be preheated to 200°C after it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tells you to put the food in.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I. Syntactic category posited by Chomsky in the early 1980s, heading

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phrase (IP or I-phrase) which is effectively a clause minus a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *complementizer. E.g. she married him would realize an IP within a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *CP or complementizer phrase since she married him: since she married

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: him|). Within this I itself would be realized by the tense of the verb (-ed).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I' is short for original 'INFL', itself for inflection'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: IA = ltem and Arrangement.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syllable. Borrowed into *Metrical Phonology from the definition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an iamb in verse.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iambic. (*Foot) consisting of a light syllable followed by a *heavy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ibero-Romance. The forms of *Romance, including Spanish,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Portuguese, and Catalan, that developed in the Iberian peninsula.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: IC-analysis. See constituency.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemic method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Icelandic. North *Germanic, attested from the Middle Ages by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: literature in a form described as Old Norse, at a time when the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differentiation of North Germanic into separate languages was still

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at an early stage. The spelling of Old Norse devised in the mid-12th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century, which is set out and justified in the anonymous ‘First

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grammatical Treatise', is remarkable as an early application of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic pattern.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iconicity. Principle by which semantic relations are reflected in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formal patterns by which they are realized. Thus a *direct object is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *complement of a verb while an *adverbial such as today is not: in that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense the semantic relation of verb to object is closer. In the order of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words in English, direct objects are also closer to the verbs: I saw John

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: today or Today I saw John, not I saw today John. In this way there is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iconic correspondence between the linear order of elements and their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term is from *Peirce's theory of signs, of which ‘icons' were one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kind. But linguists' usage is now largely independent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ictus. Traditionally of a rhythmical beat in a line of verse: thus in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Latin verse a stressed syllable is seen as coinciding or not coinciding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the ictus of the relevant foot.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idealization. The process by which, e.g. the elements and rules of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language are established as a system underlying the phenomena of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech. Likewise of the elements so established: e.g. a phoneme seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as an ideal sound which underlies a shifting range of real sounds and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: real mechanisms by which they are produced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illative (ILL)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ideational. (Meaning, *function of language) involving the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation of ideas. Cf. cognitive meaning; also descriptive (3)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referential, representational.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ideogram. A character in writing seen as representing an idea in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstraction from words. E.g. in '15', the number itself is represented

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independently of the relevant word in English (fifteen), or in French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (quinze), and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also ideograph': sometimes used, especially in older treatments,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for what is now more usually called a *logogram.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ideophone. Used by Africanists of a distinct class of forms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characterized by phonological structuręs that tend to be peculiar to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: them: e.g. by patterns of *sound symbolism, reduplicative structures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or distinct patterns of tones.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker and another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idiolect. The speech or 'dialect' of a single individual. Hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idiolectal variation is variation within a language between one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idiom. A set expression in which two or more words are syntactically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related, but with a meaning like that of a single lexical unit: e.g. 'spill

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the beans' in Someone has spilled the beans about the bank raid, or put one's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: foot in it' in He can never make a speech without putting his foot in it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in ordinary usage cf. accent (2); dialect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Not usual, as a technical term, in any other sense. For others current

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the idiom 'spill the beans'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'idiom chunk'. A part of an idiom separated from the rest by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactic process. E.g. in The beans were by then pretty well spilled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (meaning that some secret was out) the beans is a detached chunk

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idiophone. See interjection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: IE = Indo-European.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iff. For 'if and only if'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Igbo. The official language in south-east Nigeria, native to an area

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Port Harcourt northwards, including Onitsha, Enugu, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Afikpo. Variously classed, with others in the south of Nigeria, either

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as Eastern *Kwa or as *Benue-Congo.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'I-language'. Chomsky's term from the mid-1980s for the knowledge

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language *internalized ('I') by individual speakers. Opp. E-language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or ‘externalized language'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: house'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illative (ill). *Case whose basic role is to indicate movement into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: something: e.g. schematically, I walked house-IlL 'I walked into the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ill-formed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ill-formed. Not *well-formed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illocutionary. Applied in the theory of *speech acts to the force that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an expression of some specific form will have when it is uttered. E.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker might stop someone and say 'Please, can you help me?' By

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: virtue of its form (interrogative preceded by please) this would have the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illocutionary force of a request for assistance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. locutionary; perlocutionary. In the theory developed by Austin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and his successors, the simple act of uttering this sentence is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perlocutionary effect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: locutionary act; the illocutionary act is that of uttering it as a request;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the perlocutionary act is what is accomplished by uttering it (e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressee might ignore the request, or might in fact help). But what is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'illocutionary' and what is 'perlocutionary' plainly depends on how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: much is judged to flow conventionally from the form of an utterance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. if the chairman of a meeting says 'This meeting is now closed', this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be seen as a formula which has the illocutionary force of closing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it. But its form is more generally that of a statement, and, as made by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the chairman, it might instead be claimed to have that as its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the Philippines.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: llocano. *Austronesian language, native to the north-west of Luzon

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'image schema'. Used informally by G. P. Lakoff and others of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general concept that structures our perception of the world: e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concept of 'a container', or of 'movement up and down', or of 'a long

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thin object'. Patterns of *metaphor (2) can be seen as transformations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relating one image schema to another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: immanent. Inherent. Thus one view of a *language system is that it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a structure immanent, i.e. inherent, in the phenomena studied.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Traditionally the opposite of 'transcendent'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: immediate. Used where a relation has no intermediate term. Thus,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in accounts of *constituency, the immediate constituents of a unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are the smaller units into which it is directly analysed; in a *phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure tree, a node A immediately dominates another node B if

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are connected with no other node intervening.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imparisyllabic. Not *parisyllabic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imperative (imp). (Construction, form of verb) whose primary role is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in giving orders. E.g. Get out! is an imperative sentence; in Latin, i ‘go!'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is an imperative form of the verb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sometimes used simply in the sense of ‘order'. E.g. in Latin, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subjunctive such as eat ‘go-suBj-3sg' can be what is traditionally a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *third-person imperative ('May such or such a person go'). But, like

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *declarative and *interrogative, it is in principle a term in grammar,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the role of ‘order' being one that constructions, etc., including ones

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other than imperative, have in context.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicational scale

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imperfect (impr). Traditional term for forms of a verb that are past

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *progressive as opposed to *perfect: e.g. Latin vivebat ('live-ImPF-3sG’)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'was living, was alive', as opposed to vixit 'lived, has lived, is no longer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alive'. Hence, e.g. of forms such as English was living.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imperfective (imperF). Not *perfective: i.e. of forms used to refer to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: actions, etc. conceived as extending over a period of time,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuously or at intervals.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. progressive. In a notional analysis of *aspect the progressive in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: weekend; 'perfective' met her last weekend.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English or the *imperfect in Latin or the Romance languages can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described as imperfective, while the simple past or ‘preterite' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perfective. E.g. ‘imperfective' is courting our daughter, was seeing her every

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impersonal (impers). (Verb) which does not take a subject: e.g. Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oportet 'ought' in quid me oportet facere? 'What should I do?' (lit. 'what-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Acc me-Acc ought to-do'). Thence of the construction taken by such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a verb, and generally of constructions that are similar. E.g. It is nice

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to relax is impersonal since, although there is a subject (it), it is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dummy which does not refer to a specific individual or person'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term originates in the description oflanguages like Latin which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have subjects in the strictest sense: see subject (1). But it could in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle be extended to any in which some element is similarly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impersonal passive. An *impersonal construction in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb is passive in form. Thus in German Es wurde getanzt ‘There was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dancing', wurde getanzt is passive (lit. 'was danced'); at the same time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: es is a *dummy, as in e.g. Es schneit ‘It is snowing', which does not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: refer to something that was being danced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also of other impersonal constructions in which the verb can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as in some way like a passive. E.g. in Spanish Se venden casas

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Houses for sale', the construction with se is described as impersonal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: except that the verb venden ('sell-3PL') agrees with casas ('house-PL').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Although venden is active, its relation to casas is taken to be like that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a passive to its subject; so this sentence too is a passive impersonal'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implication. Relation in logic such that, if p is true, then q is also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: true. Commonly written p → q: e.g. 'girl (x) → female (x)' ('If x is a girl

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: then x is female'). Mutual implication, written p ↔ q, is the case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where each proposition implies the other.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicational scale. Any scale in which a feature associated with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a given point implies the presence of those associated with all lower

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: points. E.g. a scale in which points correspond to dialects, such that.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the lowest point, dialect A has undergone a sound change s,; at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: next highest dialect B has, in addition to s,, undergone s₂; at the next

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: highest dialect C has, in addition to s, and s,, undergone s3, and so on:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicational universal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i.e. the operation of sound change s, implies that of all changes s,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where j < i. Also, e.g. in cases of *gradience: thus form A might satisfy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one criterion; form B both that and another, form C both those and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Accessibility scales in syntax reduce to the same model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicational universal. A *linguistic universal of the form ‘if a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: then b'. E.g. if a language has phonetically nasal vowels, it also has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oral vowels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicature. 1. Any meaning that a sentence may have that goes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beyond an account of its meaning in terms of *truth conditions. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kind of implicature within that definition, and *conventional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicatures. 2. Also, loosely, in the sense of conversational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implicature.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes both *conversational implicatures, defined initially as one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implosive. A *stop produced by an *airstream mechanism in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: air is initially rarefied above the larynx. In the simplest case, the glottis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is closed and a stop is articulated at some place of articulation forward

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of it; the larynx is then lowered, so that, when the forward closure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is released, air is drawn inwards into the space behind it. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mechanism is, on this basis, classed as *glottalic and *ingressive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But the drop in air pressure above the larynx also causes air to pass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periodically upwards through the glottis: hence stops of this kind

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usually have an effect of voicing. A bilabial implosive [6} and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dental/alveolar implosive [d] are widespread e.g. in West African

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The terms 'implosif' and ‘implosion' have a different sense in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French. E.g. in acteur 'actor' the c [k], which ends a syllable, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'implosive'; the following t [t], which begins one, is ‘explosive'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. expletive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imprecative. A sentence, especially a *minor sentence, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes a swear word or some other form used in abuse. Hence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some, like Damn you!, which are indeed, in origin, imprecations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impressionistic transcription. A *phonetic transcription of speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: done by ear without, or as a prelude to, a phonological analysis;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternatively, one done by ear without the aid of instruments.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inalienable possession. Possessive relation in which the thing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessed is an inherent part of the possessor: e.g. in Mary's eyes,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referring to the eyes that are part of Mary's own body. Opp. alienable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possession, the two being distinguished in some languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inanimate. Not *animate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inceptive = inchoative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indeclinable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inchoative [in'kəuətiv]. (Verb, *aspect) indicating the initiation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some process or action. E.g. Latin senescere ‘to grow old' or maturescere

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to ripen' are traditionally called inchoative verbs, and -esc-, by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are formed from the words for 'old person' and 'ripe', an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'inchoative suffix'. Also called 'inceptive'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'incidence'. The range of individual forms in which e.g. a particular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound unit is found. Differences of 'incidence' have been distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in dialectology from differences in e.g. the system of sound units itself

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inclusion. Technically of a relation between sets in which all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: members of a set A are also members of a set B. If so A is included in B;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is properly included if, in addition, at least one member of B is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a member of A.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least one other'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inclusive. (Person, pronoun) used in referring to the speaker plus at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least one addressee: e.g. Tagalog kata ‘you and I’, tayo you and I and at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both opposed to a first plural.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An inclusive form used to refer to a single speaker and a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressee is often called 'dual'. One which refers or can refer to more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than these is generally called ‘first plural inclusive' (we' including

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the addressee) in opposition to ‘first plural exclusive' ('we' excluding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the addressee). But a form referring to both speaker and addressee is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: logically as much a ‘you' form as a ‘we' form. Hence a language may in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle oppose an inclusive person (speaker and addressee) to, on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one hand, a first person (speaker but not addressee) and, on the other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hand, a second person (addressee but not speaker). A language may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also in principle distinguish a second plural inclusive (you' plus the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker) and a second plural exclusive (‘you' without the speaker),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: incompatibility. (*Sense relation) among words that are mutually

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exclusive. E.g. between black and white: if something is black it cannot

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be white and if something is white it cannot be black.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: incorporation. A regular process by which lexical units which are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactically *complements of verbs can also be realized as elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within the verb itself: e.g., schematically, hunt-rabbit-PRoG-3sG 'He is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hunting rabbits, is rabbit-hunting'. Also of a pattern in which forms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appearing only as affixes have meanings which correspond to those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of forms appearing only as distinct words. E.g., schematically, hunt-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: RABBIT-PROG-3SG, where 'RABBIT' is a suffix different from, but linked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantically to, a lexical unit also meaning rabbit'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: known.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An incorporating language is one in which such patterns are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systematic: ones of the second type, e.g. in Eskimo, were the earliest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indeclinable. (Noun, etc.) which, exceptionally for the language in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question, does not have distinct inflections.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indefinite

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indefinite. Not referring to, or indicating reference to, an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identifiable individual or set of individuals. E.g. in I have to see a student,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the phrase a student does not indicate specifically which student the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker has to see: it is accordingly an indefinite noun phrase. By the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same token, a in a student is an indefinite article, someone in I have to see

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone is an indefinite pronoun, and so on. Opp. definite.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mind; but, to understand me, they do not have to know which it is.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indefinite reference. *Reference to a specific individual or set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individuals not necessarily identifiable by an addressee. E.g. if I say to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone 'I have lost a hammer' I myself have a specific hammer in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Contrast a hammer in 'I must buy a hammer', where there is no specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reference, or the hammer in 'I have lost the hammer', where the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referent is one that the speaker can in turn identify.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independent clause. A *clause which forms a sentence on its own:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence often equivalent to *main clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'independent motivation'. Support for an analysis based on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independent, or allegedly independent, evidence. Thus an analysis of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phonological system might be supported by evidence both of sound

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changes and of the progressive loss of distinctions in aphasia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as one.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Common in the 1960s and 1970s in the style of argument employed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by advocates of transformations. E.g. in They expected me to leave, me

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has the form this pronoun has when it is an object: cf. They saw me.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Therefore, in one analysis, it is on its own the object of expected:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: They expected me [to leave], not They expected [me to leave]. In addition, it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to the subject of a passive: I was expected [to leave]. In that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: respect it resembles other elements analysed as objects: therefore this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evidence might be claimed as 'independent motivation' for treating it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indeterminacy. Strictly, perhaps, of cases where a division or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinction cannot be precisely drawn. E.g. in a normal pronunciation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a word like seeing there is no way of determining exactly and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indisputably where the realization of see- ends and that of the ending

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -ing begins. Also, however, of cases where a decision will be made

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differently by different criteria. Many classic problems, e.g. of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *gradience, or in distinguishing *homonymy from *polysemy, involve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indeterminacies of both kinds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lives here. Cf. deixis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indexical. Term in philosophy for an expression whose *extension

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is relative to a specific context, with a specific speaker, addressee,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: location in space, etc. E.g. here is an indexical expression, as in Mary

layout_dets.text: Indian languages. Those of the Indian subcontinent: specifically of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *Indo-Aryan branch of *Indo-European, covering part of Sri Lanka

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and most of the area from the Indian states of Maharashtra and Orissa

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect object (IO)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: northwards; of the *Dravidian family mainly in south India and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: north of Sri Lanka; and of the *Munda family, in scattered parts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central and eastern India. Among others, English is used widely as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *second language, and also has native speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *Brahmi script, attested in ancient India from the second half of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1st millennium Bc. Modern forms include *Devanagari, used in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular for Hindi, and the separate scripts, often with characters of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very different shapes, that have developed for other major *Indo-Aryan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Muslim conquest.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indian scripts. Writing systems derived directly or indirectly from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and for the *Dravidian languages: in addition, those of *Tibetan, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of most languages in South-east Asia, including *Burmese, *Khmer,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Lao, and *Thai. Earlier forms were used still more widely, in Central

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Asia with the spread of Buddhism and e.g. for *Javanese before the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The basic type is *alpha-syllabic, as *Devanagari. The precise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: historical links, both within and outside India, are still partly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: uncertain: but for those in South-east Asia, the Mon script, attested in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Burma (Myanmar) from the 11th to the 12th century AD, and before it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Grantha script, used in the coastal area of Tamil Nadu from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5th century AD, were major intermediaries.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indic = Indo-Aryan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. (Sentence) = declarative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicative (ıno). 1. (Form of verb, affix, etc.) which represents an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *unmarked *mood in opposition to a *subjunctive, *imperative, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence that, in particular, of unqualified statements: thus Italian Entra

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Giovanni ('enter-IND-3sg John') 'John's coming in', as opposed e.g. to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subjunctive Entri, signore (‘enter-suBJ-3sG, sir') 'Do come in, sir'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indices. Commonly of subscripts or superscripts indicating whether

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrases have the same or different referents: thus Mary, said she, would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: come, with the same index'i, is a sentence meaning 'Mary said she

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Mary) would come'; Mary, said she, would come, with the different indices

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i and j, is one meaning ‘Mary said she (someone else) would come'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'indirect anaphora'. A relation between a phrase and some earlier

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression which, though not in a strict sense an antecedent, will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effectively indicate, in the light of people's general knowledge, who or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what it refers to. E.g. people know that bicycles have chains: therefore,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I was riding my bicycle but the chain came loose, the phrase the chain will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be understood, all else being equal, as referring to that of the bicycle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referred to by the earlier phrase the bicycle. If so there is said to be a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relation of 'indirect anaphora' between them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. direct object.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect object (lo). An object whose semantic role is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristically that of a recipient, e.g. to your síster in He blew a kiss to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: your sister; also, in most accounts, your sister in He blew your sister a kiss.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect question

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The relation between these sentences is often described in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dative movement. It is in part because that relation is possible that to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: your sister is distinguished, as an object, from directional phrases such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as e.g. to the seaside in He sent his family to the seaside.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect question. 1. A question as reported in *indirect speech: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where he was in I asked where he was. 2. An utterance with the force of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question which is not in an *interrogative form. E.g. the *declarative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I would like to know his name might be uttered as an indirect question,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with in part the same intention as 'What is his name?'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the person who made the promise was someone other than the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and is said to be ‘in', indirect speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect speech. The reporting of something said, thought, etc. with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *deixis adapted to the viewpoint of the reporter. E.g. He said he would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bring them might report a promise, originally 'I will bring them'. But

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reporter: hence, in the reporting, original I is changed to he. Also the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promise was earlier than the report; hence, in addition, will is changed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to would. With these adaptations, he would bring them is an example of,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: made.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. direct speech. E.g. in He said 'I will bring them', the promise is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instead reported directly, with the deixis appropriate to when it was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect speech act. A *speech act whose force differs from what is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taken to be the literal meaning of the sentence uttered. Thus Could you

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close the window? has the form of an *interrogative; therefore, in some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts, it is literally a question. The act of uttering it as a request

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would then be indirect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. indirect question (2). Other instances were given blended names

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 1970s: see queclarative, whimperative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indo-. 'In India': e.g. *Indo-Aryan. Also in names for groupings of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages form one major branch and all the other branches (Greek,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Italic, Celtic, etc.) are subdivisions of another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indo-Aryan. Branch, within *Indo-European, of *Indo-Iranian: first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attested by texts in *Vedic (*Sanskrit) from the 2nd millennium Bc,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and by inscriptions from the first.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The modern Indo-Aryan languages cover most of the north and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: centre of the Indian subcontinent, with outliers in Sri Lanka (Ceylon)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the Maldives. *Hindi-Urdu and *Bengali are by far the largest; of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the remainder, *Marathi, in the south of the main area, *Gujarati

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the south-west, *Sindhi to the west, *Punjabi in the north-west,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Assamese in the east, *Oriya in the south-east, and *Sinhalese in Sri

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Lanka all have a current literary standard and are linked to major

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: infelicitous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: political units. Others, such as *Bhojpuri or *Maithili, also have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers in the tens of millions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Across the main area, separate languages have arisen largely by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: divisions within a geographical continuum. Hence internal branches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are still not definitively established.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: common *Balto-Slavic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Indo-Iranian, *Greek, *Italic (represented by the modern Romance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages), *Celtic, *Germanic (which includes English), *Armenian,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Tocharian (extinct), *Slavic (Slavonic), *Baltic (represented by Latvian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Lithuanian), and *Albanian. Groupings larger than these are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indo-European, especially in German-speaking universities, from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
