layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level. The usual term since the 1940s for a distinct phase in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: description of a language at which specific types of element and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relations between them are represented or investigated. Thus at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level of *phonology one studies the sound structure of a language:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words or larger units are represented as configurations of units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (such as phonemes or syllables) that are specific to that level, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generalizations are stated about relations among them. At the level

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *syntax, sentences are represented as configurations of words or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphemes standíng in specific constructions in relation to other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such units. Each level is treated in at least partial abstraction from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others. Thus the phonological structure of a word is in general not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relevant to its role in syntax; the precise construction in which a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stands is equally not relevant, in general, to its phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theories of levels, whether of analysis or of representation, are an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important part of *structural linguistics, especially in the middle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decades of the 20th century. Some distinguish ordered series of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: procedures, in which one phase of analysis must precede another:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus, in particular, that of(Zellig) Harris and other *Post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfieldians. Others present a hierarchy of supposedly greater or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lesser degrees of abstraction, ranging from *phonetics as the 'lowest'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level to *semantics as the 'highest'. In many of these, levels are defined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the different *components (2) of an integrated generative grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. plane; stratum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: levelling. Historical process by which e.g. a morphological formation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: becomes regular for all relevant instances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level ordering. Grouping of processes into successive blocks, such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that all those of block a must apply before any of those of block b.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Argued, in particular, for processes of affixation. E.g. dis- in disloyal or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -ic in graphic can be assigned to an inner group of affixes: call this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: group 'class 1'. But un- in unhappy or -ness in happiness are among those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that can be assigned to an outer group: call this 'class 2'. In the model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of level ordering all processes that add a class 1 affix would apply

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: before any adding a class 2 affix: hence, it would be argued, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level-skipping

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possible to form words such as un-dis-loyal or graph-ic-ness (class 2

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affixation following class 1 affixation), but there are no words in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dis-un- or -ness-ic (class 1 affixation following class 2 affixation).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Level ordering is central to *Lexical Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level-skipping. Term in e.g. *Tagmemics for a case in which a unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of one rank in a hierarchy of size-levels functions directly in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction of one at least two ranks above. Thus the levels of word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and phrase are ‘skipped' if a morpheme is seen as entering directly, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a morpheme, into the structure of a clause.

layout_dets.text: a language or a general theory of language can achieve. In Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adequate if it generates the sentences of a language correctly, and is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correctly. A theory of grammar is explanatorily adequate if it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explains how speakers can arrive at a descriptively adequate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowledge of their language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexeme. 1. A word considered as a lexical unit, in abstraction from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the specific forms it takes in specific constructions: e.g. the verb ‘sing'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or 'to sing', in abstraction from the various *word forms sing, sings,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sang, sung, singing. 2. Any other unit, e.g. a *morpheme, seen as having

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *lexical rather than *grammatical meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical. Belonging to, or involving units that belong to, the *lexicon.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. a lexical entry is an entry in the lexicon; a lexical item or lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit is a word, etc. which has such an entry; rules are lexically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: governed if they apply only to structures including certain lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical ambiguity. Ambiguity explained by reference to lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings: e.g. that of I saw a bat, where a bat might refer to an animal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or, among others, a table tennis bat. Cf. grammatical ambiguity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical category. A class of units which have *lexical meaning or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are, in general, treated in the *lexicon: e.g. noun as a category of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words or morphemes such as tree or sky.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Used in *Government and Binding Theory specifically of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: respects. So, at a given moment, (a) some words will have changed, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Lexical Phonology. Model of morphology and phonology developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 1980s in a partial reaction to classical *Generative Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from other consonants. One need simply indicate that the initial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segment is consonantal; and, since the next two are also consonantal,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the other features follow automatically.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extension of the same technique.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by *lexical rules and by features shared at various levels.

layout_dets.text: Meillet, Antoine (1866-1936). French Indo-Europeanist, an early

layout_dets.text: pupil of Saussure, whose Introduction à l’étude comparative des langues

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indo-européennes (1st edn. 1912), with works on Armenian and other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branches, is still indispensable. Important as an organizer of French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics in the first part of the 20th century: also as a general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguist many of whose ideas have later been developed by others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus he is the acknowledged source for Bloomfield's and through him

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many current definitions of the sentence; also for the notion of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *grammaticalization (2), identified by him but developed particularly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Melanesia. Group of islands in the south-west Pacific running from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: New Guinea in the west to Fiji in the east. The languages of New

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Guinea are mainly grouped as *Papuan, with some in smaller

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: islands to the west and east. The other languages of Melanesia are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Austronesian, mainly *Oceanic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meliorative = ameliorative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposite of *strident.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mellow. Jakobson's term for a *distinctive feature that is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: melody units. Originally of phonological features assigned in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Autosegmental Phonology to the *segmental tier: cf. skeletal tier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Menomini. *Algonquian language of the peninsula between Lake

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Michigan and Lake Superior, studied in detail by Bloomfield.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentalism. Applied by Bloomfield to the traditional view that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mind is a non-physical entity controlling but distinct from the body;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed by him to *mechanism or physicalism. Later applied,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially by linguists who attacked Bloomfield and his followers,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: merely to the view that the mind is a legitimate object of study.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mental lexicon. A *lexicon as assumed by psycholinguists to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represented in the minds of speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: garden.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mention. The use of a word, etc. to refer to itself. Opp. use: e.g. cat is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mentioned' in What is the definition of 'cat'?; it is ‘used' in The cat is in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metanalysis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: merger. Change by which two units, etc. that were once distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become one. Especially in phonology: e.g. voiceless [m] in white [mait] or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which {mitf] has merged, for many speakers, with voiced [w] in wight

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [wait] or witch [witf]. Opp. split.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Meroitic. Ancient language of north Sudan, attested by inscriptions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the early 1st millennium AD. The writing system is derived from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of Egyptian, but virtually alphabetic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meronymy. Relation between lexical units where the objects,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. denoted by one are parts of those denoted by the other: e.g. sleeve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a meronym of coat, dress, or blouse. Cf. synecdoche.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Meso-American. See Central American languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a *basilect. From Greek mesos ‘middle'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mesolect. Variety of a language intermediate between an *acrolect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metagrammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meta-. Prefix used in terms for constructs or investigations on a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher plane or of a higher order of abstraction. Thus a *metalanguage

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a 'language' of a higher order than its object language; a *metarule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a higher-order rule; a set of metarules can be said to form a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Some terms are specific to linguistics, others more general. If a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar is a theory about a language, a theory of grammar is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correspondingly a metatheory. A study of the character of a science,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. linguistics, is a 'metascience'. A higher-order explanation of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principles of syntax might be called a 'metasyntax', and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the object language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metalanguage. A language used to make statements about a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language. The language about which they are made is correspondingly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Typically of artificially constructed systems. E.g. in the programme

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *generative grammar as conceived by Chomsky in the 1950s, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of grammar can be said to specify a formal metalanguage in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which rules which form the grammar of a specific object language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (English, French, etc.) are written. But languages in the ordinary sense

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are also used 'metalinguistically'. Thus a Spanish grammar of English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: uses Spanish, or a variety of Spanish, as a metalanguage for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: description of English; in an English grammar written in English, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same language is both metalanguage and object language; if someone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: says, e.g. that cough is pronounced [kpf] they too are making a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'metalinguistic' statement about that word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metalinguistic. *Function of language in referring to itself; cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metalanguage. Called by Jakobson the 'metalingual' function.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metalinguistics. See microlinguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metanalysis. Change in the position of a word boundary. E.g. ewt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: became newt by a shift of the boundary in an ewt, napron became apron

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the opposite shift in a napron.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metaphony

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metaphony [mε'tafəni). Sound change in which one or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonetic features of a vowel come to match those of a vowel in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjacent syllable: thence of phonological processes that result from it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or are formally similar. *Umlaut is one of the commonest; see also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowel harmony.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metaphor. 1. *Figure of speech in which a word or expression

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: normally used of one kind of object, action, etc. is extended to another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This may lead to metaphoric change in meaning: thus what is now

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the normal sense of lousy is in origin a metaphorical extension from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the basic sense ‘full of lice'. 2. Used by G. P. Lakoff in the 1980s of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general pattern in which one domain is systematically conceived and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken of in terms of another. E.g. terms directly applicable to war, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one domain, are systematically applied to that of courtship: She was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schema.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: besieged by suitors, I have lost count of her conquests, and so on. Cf. image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. to make it fit a line of verse.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metaplasm. Ancient term for any alteration in the form of a word,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from those for the active.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metarule. A higher-order rule expressing a generalization over a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of lower-order *rules (2). Central especially to *Generalized Phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Structure Grammar. For example, a set of phrase structure rules will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specify the structure of the verb phrase in active sentences. Another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set might specify that of verb phrases in the passive. But there are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systematic correspondences between them; accordingly they can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related by a metarule which, in effect, derives the rules for the passive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used for similar ends.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. rule schema. *Lexical rules are also a form of metarule, often

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and as wæps or wæfs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metathesis [me'taθəsis]. Change or process by which the order of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successive sounds is changed. E.g. wasp derives from a metathesized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form, with s before p, of a word attested in Old English both as wæsp

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metonymy [mε'tpnımi]. *Figure of speech in which a word or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression normally or strictly used of one thing is used of something

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: physically or otherwise associated with it: e.g. the Pentagon (strictly a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: building) when used of the military inhabiting it. This may lead to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metonymic change of meaning: e.g. the sense of bureau changed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successively from ‘cloth used to cover desks', first to 'desk' itself, then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to ‘agency, etc. (working from a desk)'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Defined in the most general sense as any figure based on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'contiguity': as such often taken to include e.g. *synecdoche: opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in this sense to *metaphor as a figure based on ‘similarity'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metrical grid. See Metrical Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Micronesia

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Metrical Phonology. Model developed by various scholars from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: late 1970s, in which accentuation in English and other languages is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explained in terms of a hierarchy of strong and weak units. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustration, the first syllable of maker is strong (s), the second weak

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (w); in addition, maker as a whole is strong in relation to cuckoo clock.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Therefore ma- is the most prominent syllable of the phrase. Within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cuckoo clock, cuckoo and cu- are in turn strong in relation to clock and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -ckoo. Therefore cu- is the next most prominent syllable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished from earlier accounts in *Generative Phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by an insistence that stress is a matter of relative prominence, not a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is shown by a 'metrical grid', in effect a bar chart representing a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence of syllables in time on the horizontal dimension and their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative prominence by the height of bars on the vertical dimension.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *distinctive feature with absolute values. In early accounts the pattern

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A tree structure in Metrical Phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metrics. The study of metre in poetry, in part as it reflects the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological structure of syllables and words in relevant languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Hmong-Mien'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Miao-Yao. Family of languages in south China and the north of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indochina. Hmong or Miao is the largest and belongs to one branch;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mien or Yao is the main member of the other. Also called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: microlinguistics. The study of *language systems in abstraction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from whatever is seen as lying outside them. Coined by G. L. Trager in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the late 1940s, and defined as excluding the study of meaning: that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belonged instead to a separate field of 'metalinguistics', seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relating the formal system of language to other cultural systems'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Later redefined by other criteria, e.g. as the study of language systems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in distinction from that of *paralanguage.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Micronesia. Area in the west Pacific including the Gilbert and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Marshall Islands, the Caroline Islands, and the Marianas. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages are *Austronesian, mostly of the *Oceanic branch.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mid. (Vowel) intermediate between *open (or low) and *close (or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high). E.g. in the production of [ε] in pet the position of the lower jaw

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the body of the tongue is between those for [a] in pat (open, low)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and for [ı} in pit (close, high).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: middle. Originally of forms of verbs in Ancient Greek whose sense

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was broadly reflexive: e.g., schematically, I bought-MıdDLE house 'I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bought myself a house'. Called 'middle' because seen as intermediate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between active and passive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning 'can be cut easily'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence of similar *reflexive forms in other languages. Also of verbs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in *intransitive constructions that are understood reflexively: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shaved in I shaved, meaning 'I shaved myself'. Also of intransitives with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a passive-like relation to their subject: e.g. cuts in This stone cuts easily,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Middle English (ME). Conventional term for the period in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: history of English between the Norman conquest (1066) and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accession of Henry VII (1485).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diagram from front to back.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mid-sagittal. (Plane) dividing the body into equal left and right

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: halves. Hence the plane on which the vocal tract is represented by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *onomatopoeia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mimesis. Imitation: e.g. forms of words are mimetic in cases of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: path sentences.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Minimal Attachment Principle. Principle in psychological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theories of speech processing, by which, in parsing a sentence,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successive words are construed in ways which lead to minimal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: additions to already established levels of phrase structure. An

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explanation, it has been claimed, for the phenomenon of *garden

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minimal free form. A *word as defined by Bloomfield in the 1930s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. singing is *free (1) in that it can form an utterance on its own: A.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'What are you doing?' B. 'Singing.' So is sing: 'Sing!' But -ing is not:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore singing is a minimal free form, in that it cannot be analysed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exhaustively into smaller units each of which is itself free.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'minimalism'. Programme for *Principles and Parameters Theory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed by Chomsky in the early 1990s, which initially assumed no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more than a necessary minimum of types of statement and levels of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation. Specifically, there has to be some level (call it *Logical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Form) at which an *internalized language interfaces with systems of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning seen as lying outside it. There has to be another level (call it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Phonetic Form) at which it interfaces with phonetic systems also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lying outside it. There has to be a *lexicon, from which many of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properties both of Logical Forms and of Phonetic Forms will flow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There will be further conditions, expressed as output conditions or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mixing of levels'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *filters, on representations at each level. But it was then an empirical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question, to be investigated in this programme, whether and what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other forms of statement, or levels of representation, are needed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Increasingly, by the mid-1990s, a label for current formulations of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Principles and Parameters Theory, much as 'Government and Binding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory' was used as a general label in the 1980s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minimal pair. A pair of words distinguished by a single phoneme:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. tip [tip} and pip [pip}. A pair test is a test in which speakers of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language are presented with possible minimal pairs and asked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whether they are the same forms or different.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minimizer. See intensifying.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a class of *exceptions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minor rule. One restricted to a small class of units: thus especially to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: us, Jane rescues us, God rescues us, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minor sentence. Any sentence in whose construction words are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: limited to specific combinations: e.g. an exclamation like God help us!,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose construction, with 'subjunctive' help, is restricted in normal use

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to this and a few other fixed expressions. Major sentences are of types

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which are not so limited, e.g. a declarative like God helps us: cf. Jane helps

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but a major in others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minor word class. A word class which is *closed, or whose members

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are seen as having *grammatical meaning as opposed to lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning. E.g. articles belong to a minor word class, or a minor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *syntactic category; prepositions form a minor class in some accounts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minuscule. Not *majuscule.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: MIT = Massachusetts Institute of Technology: hence in reference to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: school of Chomsky, who has worked there since the 1950s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrated.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mixed language. 1. One which could be classed genetically, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equal plausibility, in more than one way. Often in the assertion that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: no language is in fact mixed in this sense. 2. One whose vocabulary is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: historically from one source, but whose grammatical structure is from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another. The extreme case is again more hypothetical than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mixe-Zoquean. See Central American languages.

layout_dets.text: model. Often of a general way of conceiving or describing some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspect of one's subject-matter. Thus a model of sound change is a view

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of how, in general, such change takes place; hence, in addition, a way

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which particular changes may be described. A model of syntax is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similarly a general view of the relations in which words stand, of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rules that govern these relations, etc.; hence, again, a pattern that may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be followed in describing the syntax of particular languages. 'Model',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in this sense, is often harmlessly interchangeable with 'theorv'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also in the sense of e.g. a computer model. Thus a system for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *parsing in computational linguistics might be seen as ‘modelling', or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is perceived. Distinguished, in this case, from a theory: thus it would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not follow, and might not be claimed, that such a model was part of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correct view of perception.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences are interpreted as true or false in such a model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. Montague Grammar.

layout_dets.text: modification (1). Type of syntactic construction in which a *head is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called ‘attribution'; the accompanying element (in this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example white) is a modifier (or ‘attribute'). Cf. complement,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementation.

layout_dets.text: Modistae. School of grammarians centred on Paris in the second half

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the 13th century. Named after a tripartite theory of 'modes', of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *accidents, based in detail on the same underlying philosophy, leads

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: account or model of syntax. Opp. multistratal.

layout_dets.text: Montague Grammar. Treatment of syntax and semantics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developing work by R. Montague before his death in the early 1970s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Based on the belief that the techniques of *formal semantics, familiar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in application to artificial systems of logic, were equally appropriate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to languages in the ordinary sense. Hence for any language (a) a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of syntactically well-formed expressions had to be specified by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formal system of syntax; (b) these expressions had to be assigned

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interpretations in an appropriate system of logic. In Montague's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: account, the syntactic categories were those of a *categorial grammar,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the form of rules combining categories being, however, essentially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unconstrained. In addition, each syntactic rule was associated with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic rule that derived the semantic interpretation of its output

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the semantic interpretations of its inputs. In later work, both the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: application of formal semantics and this *rule to rule hypothesis have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been associated with more restricted systems of syntax, especially in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mood. Grammatical category distinguishing *modality. Originally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an inflectional category of verbs in Greek and Latin, opposing in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular *indicative and *subjunctive: thence of other systems of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: modality marked by verbs, of distinctions in modality between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions, and so on. 'Modality' and 'mood' are therefore used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the same sense, by different scholars, in some contexts.

layout_dets.text: mora

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mora. A unit of syllable weight applicable to languages in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: long or *heavy syllables are distinguished from short or light syllables.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Different measures have been proposed; but e.g. a syllable ending in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: short vowel might have one mora and one which ends in a long vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or a consonant two morae.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Moré. See Gur.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morph. The smallest sequence of phonological units into which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words are divided in an analysis of morphemes. Thus the form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [anstretft] (unstretched) will be divided into the morphs [an], realizing a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: negative morpheme, [stretf], realizing the root morpheme 'stretch',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [t), realizing e.g. the past-tense morpheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is composed of morphemes realized by dis-, taste, and -ful.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme. A unit of grammar smaller than the word. E.g. distasteful

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to lexical meaning. The original sense, still current in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French: opp., in French, 'lexème' (earlier ‘sémantème'); cf. moneme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Any configuration of phonological units within a word which has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term was introduced in the late 19th century, and has had three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: main senses. 1. A unit smaller than the word which has *grammatical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either grammatical or lexical meaning: thus, in distasteful, any of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequences [dıs], [teist], and [fəl} or, in a *basic form, [ful}. Cf. morph.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3. An invariant lexical or grammatical unit realized by one or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: configurations of phonological units. E.g. [dis] in distasteful might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as one realization of a more abstract ‘negative' morpheme also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized, e.g. by [an] in unpleasant. Cf. allomorph.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sense 1 is virtually obsolete in English-speaking countries, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usage has tended to hover between sense 2 and sense 3.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme-structure rule. Used in the 1960s of a form of *lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: redundancy rule by which features were added to *underspecified

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representations, in the lexicon, of the phonological forms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphemes. A morpheme-structure condition was a *filter that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could apply equivalently to representations that were fully specified.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphemics. *Morphology, conceived as a branch of linguistics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which takes the morpheme as its basic unit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological processes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpholexical rule. A rule for *allomorphy stated over the lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entries for individual morphemes, ahead of rules which specify

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphological process. Any of the formal processes or operations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which the forms of words are derived from *stems or *roots. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reran is derived from the root run by two morphological processes,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one adding re- (run → rerun), the other changing u to a (rerun • reran).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For types of morphological process see affix; compound;

layout_dets.text: morphophonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphologization. Process of *grammaticalization (2) which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results specifically in what was formerly a word becoming an element

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphology. The study of the grammatical structure of words and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the categories realized by them. Thus a morphological analysis will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: divide girls into girl and -s, which realizes ‘plural'; singer into sing and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -er, which marks it as a noun denoting an agent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A category is 'morphological' if it is realized within words. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphological case is *case as realized by different elements within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns or words of other classes, as opposed to *case roles realized by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independent words or word order; a morphological causative is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *causative form of a verb as opposed to a causative construction, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphoneme = morphophoneme; likewise morphonemics,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphonology = morphophonemics, morphophonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but [əuf] (oaf) + plural is unchanged.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophoneme. Unit posited in the 1930s to account for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternations in morphology which are *recurrent but not *automatic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. knives or loaves has a [v] ( [naıv], [ləuv]) where knife or loaf has an [f].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The alternation is recurrent, since it is found in more than one word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But it is not automatic, since it is not found e.g. in oaf and oafs, both of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which have [f], or in hive and hives, both of which have [v]. To account

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for it, forms such as knife and loaf are said to end in a morphophoneme

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'F’, identical to [f] except that, when the plural ending follows, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized by [v]. Thus, in terms of processes, [naıF] + plural -→ [naiv]-.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in wreath (plural [ri:∂z]).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Usually written, as here, with a capital letter. But, like phonemes,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophonemes can be analysed into features. E.g. 'F' might have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the same phonetic features as [f] plus a *diacritic feature which may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be said to 'trigger' the alternation. The same diacritic feature might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also distinguish a morphophoneme 'S' in house (plural [hauziz) or ‘Θ'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophonemics. See morphophonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophonemic script. See phonemic script.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophonology. Branch of linguistics concerned with rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or alternations intermediate between *morphology and *phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Called 'morphophonemics' by most linguists in the USA, and defined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by C. F. Hockett in the 1950s in a sense that covered the entire relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between representations of sentences in terms of *morphemes (3) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their representations in terms of *phonemes. Usual definitions are less

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wide: thus, in particular, a morphophonological rule or alternation is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one which (a) applies to phonological elements, but (b) applies only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: under certain morphological conditions. E.g. in capacious vs. capacity,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [eı] (in cap[eı]cious) alternates with {a] (in cap[a]city). The alternation is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphosyntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not restricted to this pair of forms: compare ver[er]cious and ver[a]city, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: loqu[eı]cious and loqu[a]city. Thus (a) it concerns the vowels [eı] and [a],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not the form capac- as a whole. But (b) it applies to words with a certain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphological structure, basically derived from that of Latin.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Therefore, in many accounts, it is morphophonological, not simply

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. morphophoneme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphosyntactic. (Category, feature) distinguishing forms within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an inflectional *paradigm. Thus the paradigms of nouns in Latin,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Russian, and many other languages have two dimensions, formed by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the morphosyntactic categories of number (singular or plural) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case (nominative, accusative, etc.).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Called 'morphosyntactic' from the role such categories play in both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphology and syntax. The term 'category' is traditionally used both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the feature that distinguishes the dimension in general (e.g. number

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or case) and the specific terms or values (e.g. singular or nominative)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: along it. Alternatively, the former is a 'morphosyntactic category',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while the latter are specific 'morphosyntactic features' (or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'morphosyntactic properties’). E.g. Latin puellam ‘girl-Accsg' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characterized by the morphosyntactic features accusative (Acc) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: singular (sG), which are terms respectively in the morphosyntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories of case and number. Alternatively, again, a category as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whole may be represented as a variable *feature which has two or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more values: e.g. number in Latin as the binary feature {± plural).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphosyntactic word. A representation of a word in terms of its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical properties, as opposed to a phonetic or written *word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form. E.g. 'the past tense of run' or 'run-PAsT' is the morphosyntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word realized by the word form ran.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphotactics. The study of relations of sequence, etc. among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *morphemes. Thus it is an aspect of the morphotactics of English that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. the prefix un- (in unkind or unhinge) comes before the form to which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is added. Usually of the arrangement of morphemes within words,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but also of their relations within sentences, if morphemes are taken to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be the smallest syntactic units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphotonemics. *Morphophonology or morphophonemics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involving alternations of tones in *tone languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mother'. Relation of a *node in a *phrase structure tree to any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'daughter' node that it immediately *dominates.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘caretaker speech'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: motherese. Form of speech used especially by mothers in talking to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very young children: also called 'baby-talk', 'caregiver speech',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mother-in-law language'. See avoidance style.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Munda

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mother tongue' = native language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: motivation. The opposite of *arbitrariness. Thus the relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between form and meaning is motivated, or partly motivated,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a case of *onomatopoeia; also e.g. where forms are derived by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantically regular process of *word-formation. See also iconicity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Motu. *Austronesian language in the region of Port Moresby; Hiri

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Motu or 'Police Motu' is a simplified or pidginized form still spoken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widely in Papua New Guinea.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: move α. A principle in *Principles and Parameters Theory by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any element can be moved to another syntactic position, subject to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific instances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restrictions imposed either by other principles or parameters or in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement rule. Any *rule (2) formulated as a process by which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit is moved: e.g. one of *wh-movement. A movement chain is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formed, in *Government and Binding Theory, by the linkages between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a unit and successive *traces left in positions from which it is moved.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mu (μ). Symbol for a *mora.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multi-. From the Latin word for 'many': cf. poly-.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multilateral comparison = mass comparison.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation. Opp. bilateral.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multilateral opposition. One between terms distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by more than one feature. Especially of phonemes: e.g. [p] and {s] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English are in a multilateral opposition, since they are distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within the consonant system by both place and manner of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multilingual. 1. (Person) having equal control of more than two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native languages. 2. (Community) in which more than two languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are native. Thence loosely, as *bilingual, e.g. of someone who has some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: command of more than two languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multiplex. See social network.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multistratal. Having a series of *levels of representation. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory in the 1980s assumed a multistratal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model of syntax. Opp. monostratal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multivalued. Not *binary. Thus a multivalued feature is one whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values are not simply ‘+' and ‘-': e.g. that of vowel height if it is seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involving a *gradual opposition. Likewise a multivalued logic is one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which propositions may be other than just true or false.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Munda. Family of languages spoken in scattered areas of central and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: eastern India: a proposed branch of *Austro-Asiatic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: murmured

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: murmured. Articulated with breathy voice: i.e. with the vocal cords

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vibrating but in a position that allows an airflow greater than in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *voiced sounds. The h in ahead is typically murmured: phonetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: {ə'hεd}. Murmur is distinctive for stops in e.g. Hindi-Urdu, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those called 'voiced aspirates' are murmured [b], [dⁿ], etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Muskogean. A small family of languages native to parts of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: south-eastern USA, from Texas to Florida. Choctaw (Mississippi) is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the least moribund.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between phonemes. Specifically, in Celtic, of grammatically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of words. E.g. basic [k} in Welsh cath 'cat' [ka:θ] → {g} in y gath 'the cat

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [ə ga:θ]; [nh] in fy nghath i 'my cat' [ən gha:θ i]; [x] in ei chath hi 'her cat'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mutation', and 'spirant mutation'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mutation. Generally, of sound changes that lead to alternations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditioned alternations of consonants, especially at the beginnings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [i xa:θ hi]. These are instances of, respectively, 'soft mutation', 'nasal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'silent'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mute. An old term for an *oral stop. Defined in antiquity as one that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could not be uttered without an accompanying vowel: hence, in itself,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completely.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mutual knowledge. The knowledge that a speaker and addressee

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are seen as jointly taking for granted at a given point in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interchange. E.g. if A says to B 'Jones is coming', one condition for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successful communication is that A and B should share the knowledge

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of who Jones is: specifically, B knows who A means by Jones', A knows

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that B knows this, B knows that A knows that, and so on. Often in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts which argue that complete success in communication is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possible if but only if all relevant knowledge is shared, in this sense,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called 'shared knowledge'; cf. background knowledge.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mutually intelligible. (Dialects, languages) each of which can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be understood, or understood sufficiently for ordinary purposes, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers of the other: e.g. Danish and Norwegian or, to a lesser degree,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Danish and Swedish. Often seen as a necessary property of *dialects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mycenaean. Form of Greek attested in the 2nd millennium BC, on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the site of Mycenae and elsewhere, by records in *Linear B.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: N

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: N. 1. = noun. 2. = nasal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Na-Dené. Conjectural family linking *Athabaskan with three other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: North American languages (in ascending order Eyak, Tlingit, Haida).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Proposed by Sapir; still contested.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nahuatl. *Uto-Aztecan language, spoken in various parts of central

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mexico. The language of the Aztecs; important also as a second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language before and after the Spanish conquest. Written at the time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the conquest in a script derived from the *Mayan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narratology. The formal analysis of narrative texts, on lines inspired

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by or seen as similar to European structural linguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Narrow Bantu = Bantu.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Narrow Romic. See Sweet.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transcription.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narrow transcription. A phonetic transcription which is detailed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: down to the level at which features can be distinguished. Thus a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narrow transcription of one pronunciation of stray might be expected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to indicate that the stop is released by a fricative, that the place of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation of [s] is slightly backer than in say, that in all three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants the lips are rounded, and so on. Opp. broad

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages. Opp. wide vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narrow vowel. One in whose production the tongue is bunched

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards the centre so that its upper surface is relatively convex in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cross-section. A possible factor in distinguishing e.g. [i:] from [1] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, or in similar distinctions in other northern European

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nasal. Produced with lowering of the soft palate, so that air may pass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: through the nose. Thus [m| and [n| in man [man] are nasal *stops or,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if not classed as stops, are nasals; the vowel of French saint,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conventionally [ē|, is a nasal vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lowered.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. oral. The nasal cavity is the additional resonating chamber

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formed by the passages through the nose when the soft palate is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follows.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nasal assimilation. Usually of a process by which nasal consonants

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have the same place of articulation as adjacent oral consonants. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the n of unkind tends to be either velar ((g)), or to be realized with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overlapping [n} and [ņł, by *assimilation to the velar plosive that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nasalization

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nasalization. Change or process by which vowels or consonants

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become nasal. Thus, in the history of French, the vowel of Latin unus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'one' or manus ‘hand' will have been nasalized, in the context of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: following nasal consonant, before, at a later stage, that consonant was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lost: thus Modern French un (conservatively [|), main ([m]).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also of the lowering of the velum seen as comparable to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *secondary articulation. Thus 'nasalized vowel' = nasal vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nasal release. The *release of a closure by lowering of the soft

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palate, so that air passes outwards through the nose: e.g. that of the [t]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in [batn] (button). Also called 'nasal plosion'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Luxembourgish.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nationat language. One which is a source or sign of identity for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nation. Potentially distinguished from an official language: e.g. until

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the mid-1980s Luxembourg had two official languages (French and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: German), but the national language was then, as it is now,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native. (Form, word, etc.) which is not historically a result of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *borrowing. E.g. cow, which has cognates in other Germanic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages, is native to English; beef, which derives from a form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: borrowed from Old French, is not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native language. A language that people have acquired naturally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as children, as opposed to one learned later, e.g. through formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: education. By the same token they are native speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nativism. The theory that specific properties of the mind are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inherited, not acquired. Hence especially, in linguistics, of Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of the development of language in children from genetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Empiricism is the philosophical doctrine traditionally opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nativized. (Form, etc.) which is historically a loan but is no different,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nor perceived as different, from those that are native. E.g. cheer, from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the word for ‘face' in Old French, is nativized in English; rouge is not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: natural class. Any class, of sounds especially, whose members share

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some property that distinguishes it from others. E.g. in English [m], [n],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [η] form a natural class; [n] and, say, [h] do not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'natural gender'. See gender (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Natural Generative Phonology. Model developed by J. B. Hooper

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and others in the 1970s and early 1980s, in reaction to *Generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology as developed by Halle. Distinguished by a strict division

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between phonology and *morphophonology, and by attempts to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constrain either phonological rules or the forms on which they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operate by conditions which exclude *abstract representations. These

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: include a condition by which rules are *ordered only intrinsically.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: naturalness

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: natural language. 1. An imagined or invented system similar to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a language except that the relation between forms and meanings is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: natural rather than *arbitrary: e.g. one in which, say, all the words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for animals begin with b, all those for mammals with ba, all those for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: primates with bac, and so on. 2. A language in the ordinary sense,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is or has been learned and spoken naturally by a community,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to an artificial system resembling a language in one or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more respects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Attempts to develop 'languages' which would be natural in sense 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are characteristic of the *Universal Language Movement from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conversely, languages which are gratuitously described as natural in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense 2 are not ‘natural' in sense 1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mid-17th century. But these were not, of course, natural in sense 2.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Natural Morphology. A broad approach to morphology, developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially in Germany and Austria from the early 1980s, in which both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the structural tendencies of languages in general, and the specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processes of change in individual languages, are explained in part by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the operation of hypothetically universal laws of *naturalness. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is easier to understand words if their morphological structure is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transparent: hence, in particular, if categories are realized by affixes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (English bake-d or hen-s) rather than e.g. by vowel change (English took

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or men). In that sense affixation is more natural: hence, in languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally, it is the commonest process and, as specific languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change, the tendency, all else being equal, is for its scope to increase.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in the history of English, plurals with affixes, like cows, have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tended to replace ones that are less transparent, like kine. By other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed laws, it is natural e.g. that a plural, which is *marked (1) in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposition to a singular, should be realized by the presence rather

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than the absence of an affix: plural hen-s vs. singular hen, not plural hen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vs. singular hen-s. Hence, again, this pattern is found more widely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across languages, and, again, specific changes will tend towards it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Laws such as these reduce to a general principle of *iconicity. But

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one law may conflict with another, and conflicts may be resolved in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different ways in different types of language. Moreover, any law may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conflict with structures inherent in a specific system. Hence all apply,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as above, ‘all else being equal'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: naturalness. The property of rules, relations, principles, etc. that are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in some degree explicable by factors lying outside language or outside

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the domain of a *language system. Thus a bird name such as chiffchaff

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or peewit is natural to the extent that it reflects the song or call of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bird itself; a process by which a velar consonant is palatalized between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: front vowels is natural in terms of the movements that the tongue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: must make in articulating it; a principle in syntax by which words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linked in meaning also tend to be next to each other is natural in so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: far as it makes a sentence easier to produce or to understand.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. arbitrariness, in cases like the first especially.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Natural Phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Natural Phonology. Theory developed by D. Stampe at the end of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1960s, which proposed a universal set of phonetically 'natural'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processes. These were seen as genetically inherited by any child, but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variously confirmed or inhibited as a specific language is acquired.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Natural Serialization Principle. Principle proposed by T.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Vennemann in the 1970s, by which the order of verbs and their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complements, conceived as a relation between an ‘operand' and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'operators', tends to be paralleled by that of other elements seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standing in a similar relation in other constructions. Thus if, in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given language, verbs precede their complements that language will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also tend to have prepositions (operands) which precede their own

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complements (operators); if verbs follow their complements it will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tend instead to have *postpositions. Cf. VO vs. OV languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: originating in Leipzig in the 1870s. The tenet for which they are most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: often cited is the 'Regularity Principle', according to which changes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose causes were psychological.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Generative Phonology: i.e. a rule could apply only to forms which were
