layout_dets.text: involved in a relevant alternation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diagram.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: node. Any of the points connected by lines (arcs) in e.g. a *tree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: node admissibility condition. Any condition on e.g. *phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure trees by which a specific configuration of nodes and arcs is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: well-formed. Thus a phrase structure rule X → Y + Z can be interpreted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a node admissibility condition by which a well-formed tree can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: include a node X which immediately dominates (i.e. is connected by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arcs to) two successive nodes Y and Z.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noise. A sound or component of sounds that is not *periodic: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in speech of, e.g. *fricatives, such as [f] and [s} in farce, as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowels. Also, as generally in models of communication, of extraneous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound that interferes with or obscures a signal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nom = nominative, nominal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nomen actionis = action noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nomen agentis = agent noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that a language, or its lexicon, are not a mere nomenclature'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'nomenclature'. A collection of names: thus it is sometimes stressed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in particular, a nominal sentence or clause is one in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [- nominal].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominal. Of or belonging to nouns (Latin 'nomina'). Thus child in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: childish is a nominal root or nominal stem; he and the party are noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrases and so nominal constituents of He loved the party. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system of *parts of speech nouns originally included adjectives: hence,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *predicative element is an adjective or noun phrase without a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *copula. Thus, exceptionally in English, Nothing easier! In some modern

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts, the categories noun and adjective are likewise said to share a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature [+ nominal], in opposition to verbs and prepositions, which are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'anomic aphasia'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'nominal aphasia'. Aphasia characterized by *anomia: also called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multiplied beyond necessity'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominalism. The doctrine in philosophy that *universals are merely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: names (Latin ‘nomina') to which nothing corresponds in reality except

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the individual entities referred to. William of Ockham, in the early

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 14th century, was an important advocate, often cited out of context for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the dictum known as ‘Ockham's razor', that ‘entities should not be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. realism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominalization. Any process by which either a noun or a syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit functioning as a noun phrase is derived from any other kind of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit. E.g. the nouns sadness and government are nominalizations of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjective sad and the verb govern; their handling of the problem, in many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts, of the sentence They handled the problem.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominal relative clause = free relative clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominative (nom). *Case whose basic role, or one of whose basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roles, is to indicate a *subject (1) of all classes of verb. Thus, in Latin,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: miles portas claudit ('soldier-Nom gates closes') 'A soldier is closing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gates', where the verb is transitive; miles venit (soldier-Nom has-come')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A soldier has come', where it is intransitive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'nominative-accusative language' = accusative language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-. As a straightforward negative: e.g. non-distinctive features are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those that are not *distinctive; non-terminal nodes in tree diagrams

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are ones that are not *terminal; non-canonical forms are ones that do

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not conform to a pattern usual, or *canonical, in a language. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'non-past', or [– past], in opposition to past, or [+ past], sang.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specifically of *unmarked terms in oppositions: e.g. the present sing is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-anterior. Not *anterior. E.g. vowels are 'non-anterior'; also any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant whose place of articulation is no further forward than the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back of the alveolar ridge: [S], [k], [q], etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Non-Catenative Morphology. Account of morphology developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by J. J. McCarthy in the early 1980s by analogy with *Autosegmental

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology. Basically a technique for representing systems such as that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Arabic, in which, e.g. the word for 'book' (Egyptian Arabic [kita:b])

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the word for 'he wrote' [katab] have the same consonantal root

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (k . . . t . . . b) but two different patterns of vowels. In the representation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed the root is assigned to one tier, analogous to those of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Autosegmental Phonology, and the vowel pattern to another; both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units will then be realized discontinuously.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: = hapax legomenon.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nonce-word. A word coined on a specific occasion. Thus there is no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: established word bananaphobia; but it might be invented as a nonce-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word, e.g. for the condition of some person who refuses to have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bananas in the house. Hence of a word attested only once in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: textual record of a language or some earlier stage of a language:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-configurational language. One that is not *configurational:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i.e. one in which the order of individual words is *free (4), and whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences have a structure that it is hard or unilluminating to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represent by phrase structure trees. Hence 'non-configurational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure', of the structure of such sentences or of such a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-count (noun) = uncountable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gradience.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-discrete. Having no precise bound. Thus a non-discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language is one where the distinction between *grammatical (2) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ungrammatical is conceived explicitly as one of degree; a non-discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category is one whose membership is similarly not absolute; a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-discrete grammar is one which includes such categories, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: otherwise characterizes such a language. Cf. discrete; fuzzy;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-finite

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-finite. (Verb, verb form) which is not *finite: thus an infinitve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: participle, or any other form whose role is nominal or adjectival. If a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause has such a form as its central element it is in turn a non-finite

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-linear phonology. Any school or model of phonology which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: establishes basic units over a domain larger than that of an individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant or vowel. Especially those developed since the 1970s in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reaction to the segmental *feature matrices of classic *Generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: See, in particular, Autosegmental Phonology, Metrical Phonology; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prosodic Phonology, Articulatory Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-nuclear (argument, valent). See nucleus (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-restrictive. (Modifier) which does not restrict the reference of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phrase to which or to whose head it relates. In My father, who is very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sorry, can't come, the noun phrase my father will refer to the speaker's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: father, and will do so regardless of the presence or absence of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative clause (who is very sorry) that follows; therefore who is very sorry

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a non-restrictive (also called an appositional) relative clause. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjective poor is likewise non-restrictive in My poor FAther can't comE;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with or without it, the same person will again be referred to.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with grammatical Put it out.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'non-sentence'. Usually of a sequence of words that is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical (2): e.g. in the case of English, Out it put as compared

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'non-verbal communication'. Strictly, perhaps, of communication

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by means other than words. Typically, however, of communication in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: human beings by non-vocal gestures, and of so-called 'body language'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally, if it is taken to be communication'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'no ordering condition'. Proposed constraint, e.g. on *Generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology, that rules should not be *ordered except by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: application of general principles.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nootka. See Wakashan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: norm. A set of patterns in speech which are usual across a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: community, but are not seen as constrained by a *language system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus a front open vowel [a] might be distinguished, in a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system, from a front mid vowel, a back open vowel, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But within the range of phonetic realizations that this implies, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular quality might be the norm, or the norm e.g in informal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech as opposed to formal, or e.g. for men as opposed to women. A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language system might include no rule for the order, say, of verbs and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects. Nevertheless one order might be the norm, or might be the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: norm except in special circumstances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The distinction between system and norm is central e.g. to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Coseriu's account of change in language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Nostratic'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: normative. (Grammar, rule) seeking to establish or prescribe usage:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. one which recommends a choice between alternative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions, or chooses between forms in different dialects, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposes standardizations in spelling.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Norse. See Old Norse.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: North American languages. The indigenous languages of America

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: north of Mexico, now largely extinguished by the use of English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially. Genetically of many different families, some still tentative,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and at best conjecturally or speculatively assigned to larger groupings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The most northerly is *Eskimo-Aleut, from Greenland westwards to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others, in the centre.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Siberia; to its south, across Canada as far as the Rockies and in much of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the eastern USA, the majority of languages are or were *Algonquian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the east of the continent *Iroquoian, centred in the area of Lake

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Erie, is another established family; also *Muskogean, in parts of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area of much greater fragmentation in the south-east. *Caddoan and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Siouan languages are or again were spoken in the central plains;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these are tentatively, but only tentatively, grouped with Iroquoian. To

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the west, the two most widespread families are *Uto-Aztecan, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extends into parts of northern and central Mexico, and *Athabaskan,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in both the states of the American South-west and in western Canada

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Alaska. But the South-west is a fragmented area which includes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. *Kiowa-Tanoan as one smaller grouping. The Pacific area is in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: places even more so, with *Salishan and *Wakashan to the north, but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages tentatively classed as *Hokan and *Penutian scattered, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: North Germanic. Division of *Germanic whicn includes the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Germanic languages of Scandinavia (Danish, Norwegian, Swedish),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Faeroese, and Icelandic. Traditionally distinguished from East

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Germanic (*Gothic) and *West Germanic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: them is not yet resolved.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Norwegian. Either of the two main varieties of *North Germanic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken in Norway: Bokmål, derived from the written form of Danish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used before political independence in the early 19th century, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nynorsk, developed after independence on the basis of rural dialects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bokmål is used more widely, especially in writing; tension between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enthusiasts.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Nostratic'. Conjectural family of languages whose branches are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usually said to include at least *Indo-European, *Afro-Asiatic, *Altaic,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Dravidian, *Kartvelian, and *Uralic. Divers others are added by divers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of hypothesis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From Latin nostras of our part of the world'. An old conjecture, but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: despite continuing attempts to give substance to it, still the kind of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothesis one believes to the extent that one believes in that kind

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notation. Any device or convention falling within the ordinary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of this term. Thus the representation of back as [bak] is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example of phonetic notation; X-Y is the notational convention for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'between X and Y'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'notational variant'. Rarely in any precise sense. Usually of a model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of grammar, etc. argued to be in some relevant respect essentially the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same as another, at least superficially different, model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notional. (Category, distinction) defined by our perception of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: world in which acts of speech take place, independently of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure of a specific language. Thus time is a notional category: for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any act of speech, there is a time when the words are uttered, there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are other times preceding it and others that are to come. It may be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by tense: e.g. by adverbs such as today or yesterday.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represented, in a particular language, by the *grammatical category

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *tense. But time and tense are of a different order; and, although

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the basic role of tenses is to indicate time, they commonly have other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roles as well. Equally, time is commonly indicated in ways other than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For similar distinctions between notional and grammatical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories cf. e.g. modality and mood; participants vs. persons.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notional agreement. *Agreement determined, contrary to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pattern of *grammatical agreement, by the meaning of a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or phrase involved. E.g. in The council have agreed, the subject is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatically singular; therefore, by the rule of grammar that applies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in general, the verb might be expected to be has. But it refers to a body

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with several members: therefore have (as in The members have agreed) is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also, notionally rather than grammatically, compatible with it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tenses, prepositions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notional syllabus. Strategy for teaching a language based on and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: organized by the functions that utterances can have and the notional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories that their elements relate to. E.g. expressions of time might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form a single topic, not parts of disparate topics, such as adverbs,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun (N). One of a class of words whose characteristic role is as an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *argument of a verb and which is characteristically that of words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denoting concrete entities. E.g. dog or tree; also words such as music or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anger which, though not denoting concrete entities, have the same or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar roles in syntax. Nouns and verbs have been seen since antiquity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as two principal' *parts of speech, without which a sentence could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not be *complete. For similar reasons they are widely seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *substantive universals.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun class. Usually in reference to systems in which a class to which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a noun is assigned is reflected in the forms that are taken by other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements syntactically related to it. Thus the system of *gender (1) in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many European languages: e.g. in German das Mädchen ‘the girl', the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: NP-trace

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of the article ('the-NEuT') reflects the membership of Mädchen ‘girl'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the class of neuter nouns.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Often synonymous with ‘gender' (itself from a word in Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: ostension. Pointing out. An ostensive definition is one which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: points to individual instances: e.g. of chair by pointing out one or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual chairs, or of cut by performing the action of cutting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: OSV language. One in which an *object (3), *subject (3), and verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are at least basically or most commonly in that order. Opp. SVO

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'other-initiated' ('repair'). See repair.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'other-repair'. See repair.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Oto-Manguean. A family of languages in Mexico. Those of a branch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called ‘Oto-Pamean' are spoken mainly in the state of México; others in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or mainly in the state of Oaxaca.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: output condition. See filter.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overcorrection. See hypercorrection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overdifferentiation. The failure, in acquiring a second or foreign

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, to suppress distinctions that are made in one's first or native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language. Thus [d] and [ð] realize the same phoneme (written d) in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spanish; sounds similar to these realize different phonemes in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English; therefore, in learning Spanish, a speaker of English may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continue to differentiate them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overextension. Extension of a word, rule, etc. beyond its usual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: domain of application. Especially in reference to the speech of young

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: children: e.g. doggie might at first be applied not just to a dog, but to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cats and other small animals, a fur hat, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'overgeneration'. The generation by one part of a *generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar of forms that are then excluded by another. The strategy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is common especially in accounts of *derivational morphology and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *compounding. E.g. there is a process by which compounds can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formed from an adjective and a noun: black + leg → blackleg. If this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oxytone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applies to any combination it will overgenerate: e.g. white + wrist →

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whitewrist. But let it do so: forms like whitewrist are then implicitly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: excluded by a lexicon which will have entries only for the words that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: actually exist.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overlap. In the ordinary sense. E.g. in accounts from the 1940s and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1950s two phonemes are described as overlapping if one has among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contexts, an allophone of the other.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its *allophones at least one sound that is also, possibly in other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [a:| would be 'over-long'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over-long. Phonological feature of vowels standing in a three-way

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrast of duration: e.g. [a] is short, a distinct [a'] would be 'long',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overt. Not *null; not *covert.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: OV language. One in which a verb (V) follows, or basically or usually

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follows, its object (O): e.g. Japanese. Defined in some typologies by this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a set of associated patterns: see VO vs. OV languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: OVs language. One in which an *object (3), verb, and *subject (3)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are at least basically or most commonly in that order. Opp. SVO

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or I am relaxing strenuously.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oxymoron [pksi'mə:rpn]. Term in rhetoric for the deliberate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coupling of words that are strictly contradictory: e.g. in a devout atheist,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oxytone. A word, originally one in Ancient Greek, that has an (acute)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accent on the last syllable: opp. barytone.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: P

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: P. 1. = preposition, postposition. 2. = predicator, predicate (2). E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I saw him has the elements SPO (subject, predicator, object). 3. See

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patient.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pahlavi. Middle *Persian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pair test. See minimal pair.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palaeography. The study of ancient documents and forms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: writing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palaeontology. See linguistic palaeontology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Palaeosiberian'. See Siberian languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palatal. Articulated with the front of the tongue against the *hard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palate: e.g. the palatal nasal ([n]) in Spanish niño ['ninoļ 'child' or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French baigner [bene] 'to bathe'. Often extended to include *palato-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alveolars (e.g. [S} in French chanter [Sāte] 'to sing’).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palatalization. 1. Change or process resulting in a sound articulated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: broadly in the *palatal or *palato-alveolar region. E.g. the [tfl of Italian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: amici 'friends' [a'mitfi} represents the palatalization of an earlier [k] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Latin [a'mi:ki:]. 2. *Secondary articulation in which a stop or fricative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulated elsewhere is accompanied by approximation of the tongue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards the hard palate: e.g. in Russian, where 'soft' consonants, such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as the [t’] of the infinitive ending, are palatalized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palato-alveolar. Articulated with the *blade of the tongue against

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the back of the *alveolar ridge, e.g. English [f] in ship.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palatography. Any technique for recording contact between the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue and the roof of the mouth in the articulation of speech sounds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The record is a palatogram: e.g. a photograph showing where a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: substance sprayed on the palate has been wiped off. A record over time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is obtained by *electropalatography.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palilalia. Speech disorder described as the involuntary repetition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words or larger units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pama-Nyungan. See Australian languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: synchronic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'panchronic'. (Study, phenomenon) not restricted to specific points

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in time. Thus, variously, of universal properties of language, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patterns of change recurring across languages, of features of a specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language that are constant over long periods, etc. Opp. diachronic;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paradigm

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pāpini. Ancient Indian grammarian (probably c.500 BC), whose rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for *Sanskrit, under the title Așādhyāyī ('eight chapters'), eclipsed the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work of his predecessors and became the foundation of linguistics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in India. They include a detailed account of morphology and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *morphophonology, in which the basic structure of the word is clearly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set out, and which was to become a model, in the early 19th century,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the comparative analysis of Indo-European by Western scholars. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 20th century Pāņini's descriptive devices, which included the use

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *ordered rules and *zero elements, have had a direct influence on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfield and, through him, on generative grammar and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Generative Phonology especially.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: panlectal. (Grammar, etc.) embracing all varieties (or 'lects’) of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Panoan. See South American languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Papuan. Cover term for the indigenous languages of New Guinea,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: excepting a minority that is *Austronesian; also a few in parts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbouring islands. On present knowledge they are of up to 60

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: families, with no firm reason to believe that they are all genetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: para-. From the Ancient Greek for 'by the side of': hence e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *parataxis ‘arrangement alongside'; *paralanguage 'behaviour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accompanying language'. Also freely in the jargon for language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disorders: *paragrammatism; 'paraphasia' (wrong choice of words),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'paralexia' (error in reading), and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paradigm. The forms of a given noun, verb, etc. arranged

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systematically according to their grammatical features. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustration below, those of the Latin word for 'table' (mensa) are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arranged in two dimensions, one defined by features of case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (nominative, vocative, etc.) and the other by number (singular, plural).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the teaching tradition, paradigms such as that of mensa are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned as models (the original meaning of the Greek word from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which paradigm' comes) from which a pupil can deduce the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponding forms of other words belonging to the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *inflectional class. In a current account, this is one form of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Word and Paradigm morphology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paradigmatic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paradigmatic. (Relation) 1. Specifically between an individual unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and others that can replace it in a given sequence: e.g. between cat and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any other unit (dog, house, etc.) that can replace it in the sequence I saw

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the cat, or between {p] in spear [spıə] and [t] in steer [stıə]. 2. Generally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between contrasting units, whether or not they so replace each other:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. between sing and any other form of 'to sing' (sings, singing, sang,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sung).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. syntagmatic. Distinguished in sense 1 in the 1930s:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cf. associative relation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paradigm economy. Principle by which the number of major

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *inflectional classes of nouns, verbs, etc. is always smaller than it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would be if the numbers of alternative inflections at individual places

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a paradigm were multiplied together. Thus in Latin there were at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least two endings of the nominative singular, at least two of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: genitive singular, perhaps three of the ablative singular, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: So, if these alternations were independent, the number of inflectional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classes for nouns in general would already be greater than twelve. But

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in fact they are interdependent: nouns with ending -e in the ablative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can only have ending.-is in the genitive, and so on. Therefore the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: number of *paradigms, in the original sense of models for inflectional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classes, is actually quite small.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Formulated as an absolute *constraint, under this name, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A. Carstairs in the 1980s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paragoge [parə'gəudzi]. The development of an additional sound or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds at the end of a word: e.g. the [t] of pheasant (compare French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: faisan). The loss of sounds in this position is *apocope.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'paragrammatism'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'paragrammatism'. A grammatical error in the speech of someone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suffering from *aphasia, seen as an instance of a disorder also called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paralanguage. Any aspect of vocal behaviour which can be seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaningful but is not described as part of the *language system. Thus,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in particular, aspects of voice quality; of the speed, loudness, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overall pitch of speech; of the use of hesitation; of intonation to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extent that it is not covered by an account of phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: By the nature of this definition, the boundaries of paralanguage are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (unavoidably) imprecise.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paralinguistics. The study of *paralanguage.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Parallel Distributed Processing. See connectionism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parallelism. The use for stylistic effect of sentences or other units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that are parallel in form: e.g. My wife is gone; my children are drug addicts;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: my house is falling down; . .. What can I do? Constructions linking similar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: members can likewise be called 'parallel constructions': thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *coordination (cf. parataxis) or *correlative constructions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parenthesis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameter. 1. A limited range of values of some characteristic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: property. E.g. the realization of a vowel may vary within certain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameters, defined by a range of vowel heights, or of formant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frequencies, and so on. 2. A principle in Chomsky's theory of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *universal grammar which specifies a finite set of alternatives. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *null-subject or pro-drop' parameter specifies that a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either may or may not allow the subject of a sentence to be null. As

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a child acquires a language, parameters are said to be ‘set' according

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to experience. E.g. children acquiring English will develop a grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which the null-subject parameter is set negatively; hence Énglish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers cannot say e.g. Are coming for They are coming. But for children

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning Italian it will be set positively; hence Italian speakers can say

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Vengono '(They) are coming'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by *wh-movement: Which did you mark t . . .?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parasitic gap. A null syntactic element, as seen from a viewpoint

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as that of *Government and Binding Theory, which can be null

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only because it is related to another gap left by an element that has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been moved. E.g. the object of reading is seen as a null element (0) in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Which did you mark without reading Ø properly? But this is not possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when mark is followed by its own object (I marked these without reading

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properly). Therefore the ‘gap' (Ø) is said to be parasitic on a *trace left

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In ordinary terms, which is related as direct object to both mark

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and reading, or, at least arguably, to the whole of mark without reading

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properly. Cf., with coordination, Which did you mark and not read properly?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parasynthetic. 1. (Compound) one of whose members includes an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affix which is related in meaning to the whole: e.g. red-lipped = [red lip]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -ed 'having (-ed) red lips'. Cf. bracketing paradox. 2. Also, especially in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French ('parasynthétique’), of a derived verb formed by the addition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both a prefix and a suffix: e.g. re-juven-ate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parataxis. 1. The ancient term for *coordination, applied especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to that of clauses or sentences. Opp. hypotaxis. 2. A syntactic relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between successive units marked only by intonation: e.g. in I am tired,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I am hungry, said with the same intonation as I am tired and I am

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hungry. Sense 1 is the original, the term being simply the Greek for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'coordination'. Sense 2 is that of Bloomfield.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence paratactic, also in both senses.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'paratone'. A postulated sequence of units in speech, defined as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such by their intonation, thought to constitute a larger unit like a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: paragraph' in writing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parentheses (). See round brackets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parenthesis. A syntactic unit which interrupts a larger unit: e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bill—let's face it—is too young, the parenthesis let's face it interrupts the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause Bill is too young. Defined by Bloomfield and others as a form of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parenthetical verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *parataxis (2): i.e. the relation of the parenthesis to the unit that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encloses it is seen as marked in speech only by the intonation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parenthetical verb. A verb such as think that can be used in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *parenthesis like He comes, I think, tomorrow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parent language. An earlier language from which one or more later

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages (the daughter languages') are immediately descended. Cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parisyllabic. 'Having equal syllables'. Traditionally of Latin or Greek

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns which have the same number of syllables in all cases in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: singular.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also of the utterances so produced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parole. Defined by Saussure as the 'executive' aspect of language,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: past perfect: i.e. working in Oxford was over a period before some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: moment of time which is itself in the past. In I have worked in Oxford

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for three years or I have finished already, the forms have worked, have finished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are similarly present perfect: the reference is to working or finishing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: up to or before the moment of speaking. In I will have worked there for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: three years, or I will have finished by Friday, the working or finishing is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prior to a moment in the future: hence these are often described as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *perfective.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also abbreviated ‘pERF'; but this might usefully be reserved for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iterative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perfective (per). Verb form, etc. used of actions or processes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conceived as simple events located at an undivided moment of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time. Opp. imperfective; also e.g. progressive, durative, habitual,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus, schematically, perfective go-PAst-PERF-I to London 'I went to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: London' vs. imperfective go-PAsT-ımPeRF-l to London 'I was on my way to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: London'; perfective open-PREs-PERF-I the parcel 'I open, have this moment

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opened the parcel' vs. imperfective open-PREs-IMpERF-I the parcel 'I am

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: engaged in opening the parcel'. Widespread as an opposition between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related verbs in Russian and other Slavic languages: hence central in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many general accounts of *aspect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perfectum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perfectum. Term in Latin grammar for forms of the verb based on, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the stem of, the tense traditionally called 'past perfect'. Cf. infectum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'performance'. Defined by Chomsky in the 1960s as 'the actual use

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language in concrete situations': opp. competence. Used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subsequently in wider senses, of the utterances as such that speakers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and understanding of speech, and so on. Cf. parole.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produce, of mental processes thought to be involved in the production

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: utterances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performative. An utterance by which a speaker does something, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to a *constative, by which a speaker makes a statement which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be true or false. E.g. if one says 'I surrender' that is itself an act of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surrender; if one says 'I'll do it tonight' one thereby makes a promise.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An explicit performative is one in which a specific verb is used to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: make the nature of the act clear: e.g. 'I promise you I'll do it tonight',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or 'I invite you to come tomorrow'. A verb such as promise or invite is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in turn a performative verb, or is 'used performatively', in such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'performative hypothesis'. The notion, fashionable in the early

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1970s, that every sentence has a *performative verb as part of its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: underlying syntactic structure. E.g. Prices slumped derives from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure like I say to you [prices slumped]; Did prices slump? from one like

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I ask you [prices slumped], and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds. Opp. aperiodic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periodic (1). (Sound) characterized by regular recurrence of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identical wave form. Thence periodicity, as the property of such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periodic (2). Term in rhetoric for a sentence, passage, or style

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which includes large numbers of subordinate clauses. A 'period' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditionally any complete sentence: thence of such sentences in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periphery. 1. The elements of a clause other than its *nucleus or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'core'. E.g. in I sent it to London last Tuesday the adverbial last Tuesday is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a peripheral element accompanying the nucleus I sent it to London.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A peripheral *case or *case role is likewise one associated with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peripheral elements. 2. Those aspects of a grammar which, according

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to Chomsky, do not belong to *core grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periphrastic. (Form, construction) in which independent words are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described as having the same roles as inflections. E.g. more beautiful is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periphrastic form of the *comparative, in which the role of more is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same as that of -er in prettier. Likewise the present *perfect have written

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is one of a set of periphrastic forms seen as forming part of the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic system as the simple present (write) or past (wrote).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perispomenon [peris'pəumınən]. The Greek word for the circumflex

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: person

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perlative. *Case whose basic role is to indicate the course of, or a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: location intermediate in, a movement. Thus, schematically, walks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: door-PERt 'walks through the door'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perlocutionary. Term applied in the theory of *speech acts to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effect brought about by an utterance in the particular circumstances

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which it is uttered. Cf. locutionary, illocutionary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. a wife might say to her husband 'Have you remembered to mend

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the steps?' The perlocutionary effect might be that perhaps intended,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that he goes and mends them. Or it might be that he loses his temper,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or simply replies 'Yes, dear'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: permansive. (*Tense, *aspect) indicating that a state, etc. is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: persistent or permanent. Cf. durative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: permissive in You can show it to me if you like; let in They let us leave is in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: made us leave.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: permissive. (*Mood, *modality) indicating permission. E.g. can is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some accounts a permissive' *causative, in opposition to make in They

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: = progressive assimilation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perseveration. Term in psychology for repetition or continuation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A 'perseveration error' is a slip of the tongue in which a sound, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in one word is repeated in one that follows: e.g. cold curkey for cold

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: turkey. Perseverative coarticulation is *coarticulation in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation of a preceding unit accompanies or overlaps that of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit following. E.g. in boot the lip rounding of [u:), with raising of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the back of the tongue towards the soft palate, may persevere' in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the articulation of [t). Hence perseverative assimilation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The opposite of anticipation; cf. anticipatory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Persian. *Iranian, spoken mainly in Iran, where called Farsi and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native to about half the population; also forming a continuum with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dari, spoken mainly in parts of Afghanistan, and Tajiki, centred in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Tajikistan. Written in the Arabic alphabet, with minor adaptations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Modern Persian evolved from Middle Persian after the Muslim

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conquest of the Sassanid empire in the 7th to 8th centuries AD. Old

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Persian is an earlier form attested by inscriptions of the Achaemenid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empire before its conquest by Alexander.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: person. Grammatical category distinguishing speakers and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressees from each other and from other individuals, etc. referred

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to. Traditionally, a form referring to (or including reference to) the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker is first person: e.g. the pronouns I and we. One referring to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (or including reference to) one or more addressees is second person:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. you. One which involves reference to neither is third person: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he, she, it, they. Some languages also distinguish an *inclusive person,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referring to or necessarily including reference to both the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the addressee or addressees.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'personal infinitive'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term is from Latin persona character in a play' and its sense is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore like that of *participant (1). But it is helpful to distinguish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: participants as a *notional category from person as the grammatical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category corresponding to it. Thus a specific language may have a form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identifying that the speaker is involved in some way in an event

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referred to: its meaning might thus be represented, in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: participants, by a feature {+ speakerļ. But it might not be opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directly, within a single system, to other 'persons'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbours shut the door'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'personal infinitive'. A form, e.g. in Portuguese, which is classed as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an infinitive on grounds of syntax but is inflected for *person. E.g.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, I-heard the neighbours to-shut-3PL the door 'I heard the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: personal pronoun. One of a set of pronouns that distinguish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *persons: e.g. !, we, you, he, she, it, they. Often used of a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguishing reference to speakers and addressees only, reference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to other participants being indicated by forms whose grammar is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: person deixis. *Deixis depending on the identity of speakers,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressees, and others. E.g. that of I: if Bill Bloggs is the speaker it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: refers to him, if Mary Tonks to her, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: personification. Reference to something general or abstract as if

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it were an individual: e.g. love is personified in Love conquers all.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restricted.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Peters-Ritchie theorem. A theorem proved by P. S. Peters and R. W.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ritchie in the late 1960s, establishing that any *formal language that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can in general be characterized by a *generative grammar can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generated by a *transformational grammar of a kind that Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Standard Theory allowed. At the time this put paid to the hope that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *weak generative capacity of such grammars could be or had been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: PF = Phonetic Form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: PF = perfect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pharyngeal. (Consonant) articulated with the root of the tongue or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the epiglottis against or approximated to the back wall of the pharynx.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in Arabic the word for ‘eye' (Egyptian Arabic {fe:n]) begins with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *voiced pharyngeal *fricative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pharyngealization. *Secondary articulation in which the root of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the tongue is drawn back so that the pharynx (throat) is narrowed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The *emphatic consonants in Arabic are described as pharyngealized,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: though their effect on neighbouring vowels is not like that of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants whose primary articulation is *pharyngeal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonatory setting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phase. Used by F. R. Palmer and others for the opposition between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *perfect and non-perfect in English. Thus see and saw (non-perfect)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differ in phase from has seen (present perfect) and had seen (past perfect)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while differing in *aspect from is seeing and was seeing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phatic. (*Function of language) in maintaining or developing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relations between speakers. Phatic communion was defined by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anthropologist B. Malinowski in the 1920s as ‘a type of speech in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which ties of union are created by a mere exchange of words'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The phatic function was defined by Jakobson in 1960 in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker and addressee, as opposed to orientation towards either

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individually, or towards the state of the world, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: orientation towards the physical and psychological contact between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Philological Society, is the oldest in the field.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philology. Used in English both of the scholarly study of literary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: texts (e.g. 'classical philology', ‘modern philology') and in the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense as ‘historical linguistics' (see comparative philology), or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'linguistics' in general. The Philological Society is a linguistic society

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: founded in London in 1842, and its journal, the Transactions of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosophical grammar. A study of grammar based on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosophical principles conceived as underlying all languages;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cf. universal grammar (1). Applied particularly to a tradition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dominant in the 17th and 18th centuries, of which the grammars of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Port Royal and of (James) Harris are outstanding examples.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Greek.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phoenician. Ancient *Semitic language, originally of what is now

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Lebanon, spread by trade and migration to Carthage and elsewhere

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across the Mediterranean. Attested from the 11th century Bc, in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Semitic alphabet believed to be the specific forerunner of that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a pattern of sound symbolism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonaesthesis = sound symbolism. A phonaestheme is a sound or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: group of sounds, e.g. the sibilants of hiss, fizz, buzz, etc., that enters into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonation. The specific action of the *vocal cords in the production

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of speech. Phonation types include in particular *voice (1), in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the vocal cords vibrate, vs. voicelessness, in which they are open; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *creak, *falsetto, *whisper. Normal or 'modal' voice is also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished from breathy voice or *murmur; and, in some accounts,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from *slack voice and *stiff voice.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The distinction in singing between 'head voice' and 'chest' (= normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or modal) voice may be wholly or largely one of phonation, but the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: physiology of head voice is less clear.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: falsetto.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonatory setting. An *articulatory setting which involves a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: persistent feature of *phonation: e.g. persistent creaky voice or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phone. A speech sound which is identified as the realization of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a single *phoneme: e.g. [t∫], [ı], and [p] are phones which realize

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successive phonemes in [tfipl (chip). *Allophones are different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phones by which an identical phoneme can be realized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonematic. Of or involving *phonemes or other similar elements.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In *Prosodic Phonology a phonematic unit is one associated with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single position in a linear structure, as opposed to a *prosody, whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: domain is (at least potentially) larger.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. [tip] in English realizes three successive phonemes represented in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spelling by the letters t, i, and p.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phoneme. The smallest distinct sound unit in a given language:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Detailed definitions vary from one theory to another. But, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general, two words are composed of different phonemes only if they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differ phonetically in ways that are found to make a difference in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning. Thus in English, {ı} and [a} are different phonemes since, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example, [tıp] does not mean the same as [tap], nor [pit] the same as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [pat]. The individual phonemes are then the smallest units in each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word that distinguish meanings and, in addition, are realized over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinct time spans. By the second criterion [ı] and [a] are single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemes since they cannot be analysed into smaller units meeting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the criterion, each with its own distinct time span.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identified.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence phonemic; e.g. a phonemic transcription of a word, etc. is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its *representation as a sequence or other combination of phonemes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also phonemics, for the branch of linguistics in which phonemes are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemic script. One in which the characters correspond, or tend

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to correspond, to *phonemes. Sometimes called ‘phonetic': e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spelling of Welsh is 'phonetic' in the sense that, though the phonemes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Welsh are not represented unambiguously, the correspondences

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between particular letters and particular phonemes is consistent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished in principle from a morphophonemic script, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the letters tend to correspond, as partly in the spelling of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tradition of the relations between words and things. The main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relations are justified by convention only, and then the view that,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interfering factors apart, they are systematic and natural. The main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conclusion is that words cannot be taken as a guide to reality. Several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence, between what are later called a subject (e.g. Theaetetus in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can a linguistic expression be seen as true (Theaetetus is indeed flying)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
