layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: position after [s]. Likewise ‘positional allophone'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: position of neutralization. See neutralization.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to happier or happiest.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positive. 1. = affirmative: e.g. I am coming is a positive sentence, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrast to the *negative I am not coming. 2. (Adjective or adverb) not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: marked for a *grade of comparison: e.g. happy is positive, in contrast

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'positive face'. See face.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positive polarity item. A word, etc. whose sense is possible in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positive sentences but not, or not normally, in negative sentences: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pretty in It's pretty expensive, where a simple negátion (It isn't pretty

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expEnsive) would be unlikely. Cf. negative polarity item.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positivism. Philosophical system developed in the 19th century by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A Comte which starts from the assumption that all knowledge is based

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on positive and observable facts, and therefore, directly or indirectly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the findings of the physical sciences. Hence, in particular, a system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that rejected metaphysics and other a priori speculation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should be falsifiable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Logical positivism was a development in Vienna in the 1920s and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1930s whose central doctrine was a ‘verification principle', by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the meaning of any statement is the method by which it can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verified through the senses. Hence statements which could not be so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verified were strictly meaningless. Positivist ideas were developed in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics by Bloomfield especially; they were succeeded, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Vienna school and, during the 1960s, in linguistics, by a different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosophy of science developed by K. Popper, in which the basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: criterion for a scientific statement is not that it should be verifiable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but simply that it should have empirical content and, if wrong.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessive (poss)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessive (poss). (Case, preposition, etc.) whose basic use, or one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of whose basic uses, is to indicate the relation between someone who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possesses something and the thing that they possess. E.g. -'s marks the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessive construction in Mary's coat; my is a possessive pronoun in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: my coat; Mary's and mine are likewise independent possessives in That

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coat is Mary's, or That coat is mine.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. genitive. Where the terms are distinguished it is usually in one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of two ways. In the first, ‘genitive' is used of a case, etc. marking in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general a noun which modifies another noun. 'Possessive' is then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used when the semantic relation is specifically one of possession.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessum) is often marked instead.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Alternatively, 'genitive' may be used specifically of constructions, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where the 'possessor' (Mary's, etc.) is marked, while, in 'possessive'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions in other languages, the 'possessed' element (in Latin,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessive compound = bahuvrihi.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'possessor ascension'. Syntactic process proposed for some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages by which an element indicating a possessor is moved

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from a noun phrase into the structure of a clause containing it:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. schematically, [My leg] hurt → I leg hurt 'My leg is hurt'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'possible world'. Any state in which the world could be: a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposition, e.g. as expressed by a sentence, may accordingly be true

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in some 'possible worlds' and false in others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. truth conditions; model-theoretic semantics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: poss-ing construction. That of e.g. John's driving in John's driving is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: terrible, jointly marked by *possessive -'s (poss) and the -ing of driving.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished from that of e.g. John driving is terrible, where john is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: post-. After or behind. E.g. a post-vocalic consonant is one preceded

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a vowel; a *postalveolar has a place of articulation behind that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an alveolar; a post-lexical rule applies at a stage in a derivation after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical units have been introduced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postalveolar. Articulated towards the back of the ridge behind the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: upper teeth: i.e. with the tongue in a position between that of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *alveolar, as in too [tu:], and a *palato-alveolar, as in chew [tfu:].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Post-Bloomfieldians. School of linguistic theoreticians dominant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the USA in the 1940s and 1950s: leading members included (Zellig)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris, C. F. Hockett, and G. L. Trager. They developed ideas derived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Bloomfield's in an extreme form, especially the principle that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *distributions of forms should be analysed independently and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in advance of their meanings, and the notion that a description

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a language could be justified by following a rigid hierarchy of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: procedures. Such procedures were later characterized by Chomsky

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as *discovery procedures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky's earliest work was heavily influenced, both in its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosophy and in detail, by Harris and other Post-Bloomfieldians.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But after 1960 he derided them as representatives of *structural or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *taxonomic linguistics, and within a few years both the school and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its direct influence diminished sharply.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'post-creole continuum'. See creole continuum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: post-cyclic(al). See cyclic(al) principle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postdeterminer. Used of an element seen as last in a possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence of determiners. E.g. in those people, the *determiner is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those. In those three people or those few people, it is followed by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postdeterminer three or few. In all those three people it is also preceded

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a 'predeterminer' all.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also, at least potentially, of any determiner that comes after the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element it 'determines'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postmodifier. In principle, any modifier that follows its head.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Specifically of an element in English which modifies and follows a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun: e.g. over there in the man over there, or who watch television in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: children who watch television. Cf. premodifier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Washington's daughter.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postposition. An element, e.g. in Japanese, related to a noun phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the same way as a *preposition, except that it comes after instead of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: before. Thus, schematically, 'of' would be a postposition in [red house)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: OF ‘of the red house'; likewise 'on' in [{[red house] oF] roof] oN ‘on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roof of the red house'. Though not usually so treated, the clitic -'s

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could be seen as a postposition in e.g. my friend's daughter, my friend in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A postpositional phrase is likewise the equivalent, with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postposition, of a * prepositional phrase.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential. (Mood, particle, etc.) indicating possibility or ability. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, You think-PoTENTIAL that ... 'You might think that . . .'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: power = weak generative capacity. E.g. *context-free grammars are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more powerful than *finite state grammars since any language that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be generated by a grammar of the latter type can also be generated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by one of the former, but not vice versa.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also, loosely, of rules. E.g. transformational rules are informally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: said to be ‘more powerful' than phrase structure rules, or to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'too powerful'. That is, more or too many kinds of operation can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be accomplished by them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: PP = prepositional phrase, postpositional phrase.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatic. Treated as belonging to *pragmatics. Thus a 'pragmatic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: presupposition'is a *presupposition that does not fall under some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restricted conception of semantics; pragmatic ambiguity is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambiguity that does not have to do with e.g. *truth conditions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatics. Usually conceived as a branch of *semantics concerned

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the meanings that sentences have in particular contexts in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are uttered. E.g. There's a car coming is seen as, out of context, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: statement that a car is coming. But in a particular context it might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a warning to a pedestrian not to step onto a road, an expression of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hope that people invited to a dinner are at last arriving, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence, in particular, pragmatics is seen as the study of *implicatures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to literal meanings' or *truth conditions of sentences.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Invented by C. W. Morris in the 1930s, for a branch of *semiotics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to syntax', seen as concerned with relations among signs, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'semantics', seen as concerned with relations between signs and their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denotata. The field of pragmatics was in turn the relations between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: signs and their *interpretants. Its use in linguistics dates from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1970s and often depends, in practice, on the definition of a narrower

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: field of meaning, e.g. one restricted to truth conditions, whose study

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatics is then seen as supplementing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prague School. School of linguistics centred on the Prague

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Linguistic Circle. Recognizable as such from the late 1920s: its journal,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Travaux du Cercle Linguistique de Prague, was published from 1929 until

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Second World War. Leading figures included two Russian émigrés,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Trubetzkoy (in Vienna) and Jakobson (then in Brno), with Czechs of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whom V. Mathesius was the senior.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: United among structural linguists by an emphasis on the *function

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of units: e.g. in phonology, on the role of phonemes in distinguishing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and demarcating words; in syntax, on the role of sentence structure in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context. Important in the 1930s above all for phonology, where ideas

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: originating in this period are the source for later work especially by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Jakobson and Martinet. A functional view of the sentence, fostered by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mathesius, was to lead in the 1950s to the theory of *Functional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sentence Perspective.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prakrit. See Sanskrit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pre-. Before in time or position. E.g. a prevocalic consonant is one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that comes before a vowel; a preterminal node in a tree diagram is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one that immediately dominates a *terminal node; the prelinguistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stage in a child's development is one which precedes the appearance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of identifiable linguistic units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preaspiration. The end of *voice (1) in e.g. a vowel before the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation of a following voiceless consonant. Thus [t} is preaspirated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in e.g. [ate] (where [a] is a voiceless continuation of [a]) or [ahte]:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common e.g. in Scottish Gaelic or Icelandic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precative. Indicating or constituting a direct request. Thus Please

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leave the room is precative in one classification of *modality.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pre-cyclic(al). See cyclic(al) principle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predeterminer. Used of an element seen as the first of a possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence of determiners. E.g. in her children the *determiner is her. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both her children or all her children it is preceded by a predeterminer both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or all. In all her many children it is also followed by a postdeterminer'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also, at least potentially, of any determiner that comes before the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element it 'determines'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate. 1. A part of a clause or sentence traditionally seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wife bought a coat in London, the subject my wife refers to someone of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representing what is said of, or predicated of, the subject. E.g. in My

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whom it is said, in the predicate, that she bought a coat in London.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. A verb or other unit which takes a set of *arguments within a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. Thus, in the same example, 'buy' is a two-place predicate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose arguments are represented by my wife and a coat.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used by logicians.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The senses are respectively from ancient and from modern logic. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense (1) cf. verb phrase, but that is sometimes used of a smaller unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within the predicate. For sense (2) cf. predicator. But that is often used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the specific word in the construction (e.g. bought); moreover it is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate calculus. Branch of mathematical logic which deals with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: .expressions containing predicates, arguments, and quantifiers. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quantifiers see existential quantifier, universal quantifier; for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicates and arguments cf. argument, predicate (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: friend in She is just a friend.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate nominal. A *predicative noun or noun phrase: e.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predication. The relation of either a *predicate (1) to its subject, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a *predicate (2) to its arguments.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'predication theory'. Usually of an account of *predicates (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicative. (Adjective, etc.) which forms part of a *predicate (1) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has a direct semantic relation to the subject: e.g. angry is predicative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in He is angry, the noun phrase a fool is predicative in He is a fool.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Predicative adjectives are distinguished from those standing in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relation of *attribution. Thus angry is used predicatively in He is angry,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but is attributive, or is used attributively, in e.g. angry customers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. predicate (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicator. An element in a clause that determines, wholly or in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part, the other elements that its construction may or must have.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Characteristically a *verb: thus in I bought a present for Zoé the verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('buy') is one that must have both a subject (l) and a direct object (a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: present), and allows a *benefactive (for Zoé). Also, in many accounts, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *predictive adjectives: e.g. mad is the predicator in She was mad at me.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predictive. (lnflection, particle, etc.) marking a prediction. Thus is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: going to might be described as predictive in It's going to fall any minute.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prefix

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prefix. An *affix which comes before the form to which it is joined:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. un- in unkind. Prefixation is the process of adding a prefix, and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prefixal form is one either derived by prefixation or occupying the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: position of a prefix. Thus, in the first sense, unkind is a 'prefixal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: negative'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: premodifier. In principle, any modifier that precedes its head.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Specifically, an element in English which modifies and precedes a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun: e.g. good in good people, broken in a broken reed, or pond in pond

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: life. Cf. postmodifier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prenasalized. (Phonological unit) consisting of an *oral consonant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: briefly preceded by the corresponding *nasal. E.g. in the consonant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: written 'nd' in Swahili, the soft palate is initially lowered, with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back of the tongue in contact with it. After a brief interval the soft

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palate is raised: thus, with voicing, [nd]. Prenasalized *stops, such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [nd], are common in sub-Saharan Africa and elsewhere; the term is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also applied to phonologically single units in which a nasal briefly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precedes a *fricative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preparatory conditions. One kind of *felicity condition that a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *speech act has to meet if it is to be appropriate or successful. E.g. if

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A asks B to open the door the preparatory conditions are (a) that B is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pro-form. Any form, such as a *pronoun, that is treated as 'standing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: she refers to will be understood from the context in which it is uttered:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in that sense, it ‘stands for' a form that would be more explicit (Jane,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so 'stands for' a form like that she would come.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Generalized from ‘pro-noun'. A form like so in Jane said so, since it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: progressive (proc). Feature of verbal forms used to refer to actions,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. seen as in progress without necessary time limits. E.g. am reading

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is present progressive in I am reading your book, was reading past

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: progressive in I was reading your book. More generally, the progressive in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English is marked by a construction in which a form of the auxiliary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'be' (am, was, etc.) is linked to an -ing form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: progressive assimilation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called 'continuous'. The distinction between progressive and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-progressive (I am readíng vs. I read) is one of *aspect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: progressive.assimilation. *Assimilation in which elements are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changed to match features of elements that precede them. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ending -s is voiced [z] in words like sees [si:z], but in writes or weeps it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assimilated to the preceding voiceless consonant ([raits], [wi:ps]).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. regressive assimilation. The sense is that of features, such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: projection of X. Phrase headed by an X. E.g. in [the [book on the table]],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if so analysed, the phrases within brackets are headed by a noun (N)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so are projections of N. The largest projection of X is the *maximal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that satisfy them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: projection principle. Principle in *Government and Binding Theory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which the range of elements with which a lexical unit combines are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: projected from the lexicon as restrictions on syntactic structures that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contain it. E.g. put takes an object noun phrase and a locative phrase:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: put [the book] {on the shelf]. These requirements will be specified by its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entry in a lexicon. So, by the projection principle, any syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure in which put appears must, at whatever level, have elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Just as a lexical unit restricts the structures that can contain it, so a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure itself is possible only if there are lexical units that allow (or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *license) it. E.g. the construction with an object and a locative (put the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: book on the shelf) exists precisely because there are verbs such as put

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that take it. Therefore there is no need to specify it or other such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: come; compare I thought he would not come.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promissive. Indicating or constituting a promise: thus will can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promissive e.g. in I will certainly help.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promotion. Syntactic process by which the role of an element is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changed to one that is seen as higher on some scale or hierarchy of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions. E.g. the role of subject is seen as higher than that of a direct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object; cf. NP accessibility hierarchy. Accordingly, a change of active to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive will promote a direct object (this letter in Mary wrote this letter) to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the subject position (this letter in This letter was written by Mary).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the passive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called ‘advancement'. The opposite process is demotion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or 'retreat'. Thus, in the same example, the subject of the active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction (Mary) is demoted to an *oblique element (by Mary)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a specified syntactic domain.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronominal. Of or belonging to the class of *pronouns (Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronomina). Both pronoun' and the feature [+ pronominal] are used in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory of *noun phrases, including some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronouns in the usual sense, that cannot have an *antecedent within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: pronominalization. The replacement of a noun phrase by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronoun, conceived as a syntactic process. Thus in *transformational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammars John hurt himself was at first seen as derived from John hurt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: John, with the replacement of the second John by himself. 'Backward

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronominalization' is the case in which the pronoun then stands in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronominal verb = reflexive verb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronoun (Pron). An element of a class whose members typically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form noun phrases whose meaning is minimally specified. E.g. she is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronoun which, ofitself, does no more than identify its referent as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single person or thing which is or is classed or conceived as female.

layout_dets.text: Traditionally said to 'stand for'nouns or noun phrases. E.g. in She

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: came, the pronoun stands for any of the more specific expressions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Lucienne, Marilyn Monroe, the girl in the corner, etc. Hence defined, partly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but not wholly by that criterion, as one of the ancient *parts of speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. pro-form: but N.B. (a) that term tends to be used only of elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that are *anaphoric; (b) a noun phrase may be anaphoric (e.g. the idiot

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I signalled to Bill but the idiot didn't see me), but not thereby a pronoun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proparoxytone [prəupa'rpksitən]. A word, originally one in Ancient

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Greek, which has an (acute) accent on the third syllable from the end.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. oxytone; paroxytone.

layout_dets.text: proper

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proper. In a strict or true sense. E.g. a *proper noun is traditionally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a ‘proper name', or name in the strict sense; proper inclusion is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *inclusion in the true sense, as opposed to identity; if by a definition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: node is one of ‘proper *dominance'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dominating itself, the relation between it and any genuinely lower

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proper noun. Noun which is the name of a specific individual or of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a set of individuals distinguished only by their having that name: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the name Mary as applied to specific girls, or London as applied to one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or more specific cities. Opp. common noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proportional analogy. Any pattern in which a differs in form and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning from b as c differs from d: in notation, a : b = c : d. The creation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of such proportions is one factor in *analogy as a process of language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analogía.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Proportion' is in origin the Latin word that corresponded to Greek

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. isolated opposition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proportional opposition. One which is paralleled by others. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a *correlation of voicing, an opposition between [t] and [d] is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proportional to similar oppositions between [p] and [b], [k} and [g}, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposition. Whatever is seen as expressed by a sentence which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes a statement. Hence, for example, the same proposition might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be said to be expressed by both I understand French and, in Italian,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Capisco il francese. It is a property of propositions that they have truth

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values. Thus this proposition would have the value 'true' if the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did understand French and the value 'false' if the speaker did not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings differ.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The 'propositional content' of a sentence is that part of its meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is seen, in some accounts, as reducible to a proposition. E.g. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: porters had shut the gates, The gates had been shut by the porters, Had the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: porters shut the gates?, If only the porters had shut the gates! would be said to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: propositional calculus. Branch of mathematical logic in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: propositions are treated as unanalysed wholes. E.g. let p be one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposition and q be another: by the definition of an operator &, p & q

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is true if and only if both p is true and q is true.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Propositions are analysed in the *predicate calculus.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proscribe. To condemn as e.g. contrary to a rule. Thus *prescriptive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: prosodic features. Stress, pitch, and length, seen as phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features e.g. in the scheme of Chomsky and Halle, *SPE.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and his followers, and distinguished from others by two main features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prosodic Phonology. Account of phonology developed by Firth

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One is the *polysystemic principle, by which the system of contrasts at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one point in a syllabic or other structure is established independently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of those obtaining at others. E.g. in a CVC structure (consonant + vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: + consonant), one system is said to operate at the first ‘C’ position,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another at the second. The other is the role of *prosodies in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounting for interdependencies between successive places in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure. E.g. in a VC structure a single prosodic contrast might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized by a longer vowel plus a partly voiced consonant (e.g. -ag in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lag) vs. a shorter vowel with the consonant voiceless (e.g. -ack in lack).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the final analysis, the linear structure can itself be seen as an aspect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of realization: thus the C in a VC structure is there precisely because

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there are contrasting units wholly or partly realized in that way.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prosodic Phonology did not develop further after Firth's death in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1960, and later theories of *non-linear phonology were at first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conceived independently.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prosody. Traditionally, the study of metres in verse. Usually, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics, of rhythm and intonation in speech: e.g. the *contour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an intonation, as falling, rising, etc., is a prosodic contour.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In *Prosodic Phonology, a prosody is an abstract unit which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized, or potentially realized, at two or more different places in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a linear structure. Thus in some dialects of Spanish a final [h] is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: associated e.g. with a relative lowering of an unstressed back vowel:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ['liβrəh] (libros) ‘books' vs. ['lißru] (libro) 'book'. Hence both features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prosody, in libros, and a 'non-H' prosody, in libro.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prospective. (*Aspect, etc.) indicating something that is about to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: happen. E.g., schematically, explode-pRosp-it 'It will explode any second'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: protasis ['prptəsis]. The *conditional clause in a conditional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence: e.g. if I had money in If I had money, I would buy it. The term

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was also the word in Ancient Greek for a premiss.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prothetic [prə'θεtik]. (Vowel, etc.) that has developed historically at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the beginning of a word. E.g. the e of establish is in origin a prothetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: protoform. A form reconstructed as belonging to a *protolanguage.

layout_dets.text: protolanguage. An unattested language from which a group

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of attested languages are taken to be historically derived. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *Indo-European languages, Proto-Germanic the source for English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the other *Germanic languages, and so on.

layout_dets.text: prototype theory. Theory of word meaning according to which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings are identified, in part at least, by characteristic instances of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their character'.

layout_dets.text: than others, such as ducks, falcons, or ostriches. In that sense, a robin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or the like is a prototypical instance, or prototype, of a bird. But birds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instance, plus other species that, to varying degrees, share some of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prototype theories are often linked with the view that denotations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have no precise limits: e.g. bats are merely less 'robin-like' than ducks,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so on. A notion of prototypes has also been applied to other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspects of language. E.g. green is a ‘prototypical' adjective, while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: asleep, with its more restricted syntax, is marginal; the 'prototypical'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of the interrogative construction is in asking questions;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: to some applications of *mass comparison, all later languages have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: expression lower on such a scale carries the *implicature that, if any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Scale and Category Grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher expression were used, the proposition would be false: e.g. if one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: says Few people came, one implicates that both ‘Many people came' and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'All the people came' are false. Such implicatures have accordingly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been called 'scalar implicatures'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise a scalar feature is a variable feature with at least one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intermediate value. E.g. if close, mid, and open vowels were terms in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *gradual opposition, vowel height would be a scalar feature: say

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [close], with the values {1 close} (= open), {2 close} (= mid), {3. close}

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= close).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Finnish and *Sami.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Schleicher, August (1821-68). Indo-Europeanist and theorist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language, whose Compendium der vergleichenden Grammatik der

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indogermanischen Sprachen (1st edn. 1861-2) played a central role, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decade before the *Neogrammarians, in clarifying aspects of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *comparative method: in particular, the technique of reconstruction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based on the postulate of sound laws, and the model of a family tree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which ancestor languages are related to their descendants. As a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general linguist, Schleicher identified the method of linguistics with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of the natural sciences, and developed a general view of language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as part of the natural history of our species into a specific model in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which individual languages were compared to specific organisms,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which they compete with one another, and in which they have a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: life-cycle of birth, growth, and subsequent decay. This was developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly in his reaction to Darwin's The Origin of Species (1859),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which itself referred to comparative linguistics as a model, and was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allied to an interpretation of the typology of languages in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *inflecting type represented a stage of perfection which resulted from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a prehistoric period of growth, followed by a historical decay into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *analytic (1) type that developed in Europe and elsewhere

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the classical and other earlier Indo-European languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In assessing these ideas one should perhaps note that when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Schleicher died he was still in his forties.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scholasticism. General term for the schools of philosophy in western

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Europe in the high Middle Ages. Important in the history of linguistics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the development of *speculative grammar, especially by Petrus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Helias in the early 12th century, leading to the work of the *Modistae

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the second half of the 13th.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary articulation (1)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Schuchardt, Hugo (1842-1927). In origin a Romance linguist, who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also published extensively on Basque and on many other languages,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including pidgins and creoles. In his general ideas, a radical critic of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *Neogrammarians (also of *Saussure), laying emphasis both on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individuality of speakers and on the continuity of usage, both within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and across the boundaries of conventional dialects and languages;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence on the diversity of paths by which changes pass from one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual to another, and the existence, at all levels, of mixing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of features from different historical sources. These ideas are most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accessible in an anthology of his papers (Hugo Schuchardt-Brevier) edited

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in 1922 (by L. Spitzer) for his eightieth birthday.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonetic notation [ə] ( [matə]). Also spelled ‘shwa'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schwa. The mid-central vowel of e.g. the second syllable of matter: in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('I think he didn't visit Mary').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scope. The part of a sentence with which a *quantifier (2), negative,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. combines in meaning. E.g. in I didn't say he visited Mary the scope of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -n't might be the main clause ('I didn't say it'). But in I don't think he

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: visited Mary it might, in one interpretation, be the subordinate clause

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term originates in logic, and its use by linguists variously

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reflects the extent to which they start from language, or start from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: translations in language of expressions in some logical system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Dutch or German.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'scrambling'. Syntactic process by which the order of words or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrases can optionally vary. Originally proposed in transformational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar by linguists familiar with languages like English, in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their order is largely fixed, as a solution for ones in which it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predominantly free. Now more usual in treating alternative orders

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a clause construction: e.g. within the basic 'verb-second' frame

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: S-curve. A graph which rises steeply in the middle, but is flatter at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the beginning and end. Claimed to be standard when the progress of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *lexical diffusion is plotted vertically against a horizontal time scale.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: At first few words are affected; hence a flat beginning. Then it rises

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more and more steeply until, when roughly half the relevant words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are affected, it again begins to flatten.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SD. See transformation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary (in syntax). See ranks (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary articulation (1). A subsidiary articulation of a speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound accompanying its primary articulation elsewhere. The primary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation is the one with a greater degree of *stricture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus the sh of English ship or shoe is a fricative whose primary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation is as a *palato-alveolar: in phonetic notation [∫]. But for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many speakers it is accompanied by a secondary articulation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *labialization or lip rounding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary articulation (2)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary articulation (2). See double articulation (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary cardinal vowels. See cardinal vowels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'secondary response'. Bloomfield's term for a statement, especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an ill-informed statement, about language: e.g. 'Working-class children

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: response' the typical reaction of someone who has made such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: know only a few hundred words'. He then described as a 'tertiary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: statement and is told that it is wrong.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'secondary speech community'. A community defined by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common use of a *second language (2): e.g. that of speakers of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English as an international language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary stress (). A distinguishable level of *stress on a syllable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other than one which carries a *primary stress. E.g. examination has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a secondary stress on the second syllable ([1g,zamı'neisn]), while

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristic, also with five syllables and primary stress on the fourth,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has a secondary stress on the first ([, karəktə'ristik]).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our entrance'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second-instance sentence. Any utterance whose intonation or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wording reflects its relationship to a sentence uttered previously: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'The `NEigíbours left it', in response to, say, 'Someone has left a van in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second language. 1. The second language that a person acquires.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus especially of *bilinguals: e.g. a speaker of Welsh may have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned or begun to learn it, as a first language, before learning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, as a second language. 2. A language which is not native to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: community but has an established role, for certain purposes or at a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: certain social level, within it. Thus especially in collocations such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Teaching English as a Second Language' (TESL).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second-order nominal. Lyons's term for a nominal expression

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which characteristically refers to events, processes, etc. as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: physical objects: e.g. his birth, his decision to leave. Cf. third-order nominal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second person (znd). See person.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Second Sound Shift'. See German.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segment. Any unit, at any level of representation, which is described

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as forming sequences with others. Thus *phonemes are in general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segments; also *morphemes. Segmentation is likewise any process,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in descriptive analysis or in speech processing, by which a form of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation at one level is divided into a succession of discrete units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at another: e.g. one which splits a representation of continuous speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into successive phonemes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmental tier. A *tier in phonological representation at which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features are associated with single consonants and vowels. E.g. in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic change

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation of end a feature of nasality might be associated only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with a segment realized by n, and a feature 'plosive' only with one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized by d.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: selection. Bloomfield's term for the feature of a construction by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which certain individual words or morphemes enter into it. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction of these apples 'selects' a determiner and a noun, and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plural morpheme in these is 'selected' in agreement with one in apples.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence of 'selection' by rule, etc. generally: cf. selectional restriction;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also c-selection, s-selection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: selectional restriction. 1. A restriction on the choice of individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical units in construction with other lexical units. E.g. breathe will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: typically ‘select' an animate subject (The girl was still breathing, Fish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breathe through gills), not an abstract or an inanimate (Theories must

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breathe, The table was breathing). Cf. collocation. 2. A restriction imposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the potential referents of a phrase, etc. related to it: e.g. pregnànt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will typically ‘select' a subject referring to someone or some animal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that is female.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammars such restrictions were seen as subject to rules, called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: selectional rules'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sense 1 is that of Chomsky in the 1950s. In the earliest generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: selective listening. Selective attention to an individual speaker, e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a crowded room where many people are talking.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: self-embedding. The inclusion of a syntactic unit in another which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is of the same class: e.g. one that-clause is part of another in the news [that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he had said [that he was coming]]. Also specifically of *centreembedding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: self-initiated ('repair'). See repair.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'self-repair'. See repair.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semanteme. Adaptation to English of a French term ('sémantème')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: originally used of a linguistic sign with *lexical meaning, as opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a *morpheme ('morphème') with grammatical meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic. Having to do with *semantics, in whatever way that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be defined. E.g. a semantic feature is a *feature by which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of a word is distinguished from that of others; a semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: component of a *generative grammar is a distinct set of semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rules that assign representations of meaning to sentences;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic criteria in linguistic analysis are criteria that make

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reference to meaning, seen as distinct from 'formal criteria',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that do not; a semantic definition, e.g. of a word class, will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: refer to types of meaning that characterize it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic change. Usually of change in the meanings of words.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Types include *extension or *widening of meaning and *restriction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic determinative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of meaning, *ameliorative and *pejorative changes; also *figurative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changes which involve a *metaphor or some other of the traditional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *figures of speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic determinative. See determinative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic extension. See extension; widening of meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic field. A distinct part of the lexicon defined by some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general term or concept. E.g. in English the semantic field of colour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *hyponyms of the more general term colour.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes words such as black and red that distinguish colours, or are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A distinction can usefully be drawn between a lexical field, as part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the vocabulary of a specific language at a specific stage in its history,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a conceptual field, postulated either as a linguistic universal or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: established across a range of languages or stages in the history of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language. E.g. a conceptual field of kinship was represented in Latin by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a lexical field which is different from any of those representing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same conceptual field in French or the other modern Romance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semanticity. The property of language by which words may be used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to refer to specific entities in a speaker's physical environment.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished as such in discussions of *design features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic loan. See loan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'distinguishers'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic marker. Any semantic *feature seen as systematic in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given language: e.g. in words like man vs. boy, woman vs. girl, horse vs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: foal, a marker ‘Adult' (or {+ Adult}) is systematically opposed to 'Non-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adult' (or [– Adult|). In an account by J. J. Katz and J. A. Fodor in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: early 1960s. features which were not seen as systematic were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be uttered.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic representation. A representation of the meaning of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence; especially one claimed to be assignable by a *generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar independently of any context in which the sentence might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic restriction. See restriction of meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic role. Usually of the roles of nouns, etc. in relation to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb: e.g. in I can feel it in my chest the semantic roles ofI, it, and in my

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chest might (in one account) be those of *experiencer, *theme (3), and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *locative. Cf. case role; theta role.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics. The study of meaning. Seen by Bréal, in the late 19th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century, as an emerging science (French ‘sémantique') opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonetics ('phonétique') as a science of sounds: similarly, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloonmfield in the 1930s, it was a field covering both grammar, as one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sememe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: account of meaningful forms, and the *lexicon. Also seen more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narrowly, in a tradition lasting into the 1960s, as the study of meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the lexicon alone, including changes in word meaning. Later, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts in which the study of forms was sêparated from that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings, opposed either to grammar in general or, within grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and especially within a *generative grammar, to *syntax specifically.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Of the uses current at the end of the 20th century, some are very wide:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus semantics will include, in particular, both word meaning (lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics') and the meaning of utterances as studied in *pragmatics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic theory' deals almost solely with problems in *formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics, even lexical meaning being excluded.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But others are very narrow: thus one handbook of 'contemporary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1920s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'semantic triangle'. Model of meaning in which a symbol and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thing it symbolizes are related indirectly via a thought or concept.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus, in the illustration, the word horse is related, on one side of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the animal itself; the broken line which forms the third side shows

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the merely derivative relation between the animal and the word. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of diagram was introduced by C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic valency. The *valency of verbs, or of verbs in particular,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in terms of semantic roles or *case roles. Thus eat and see both take a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject and an object; in that sense they have the same syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: valency. But in I am eating it the subject of eat is an *agent, while in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I can see it that of see is an *experiencer. Therefore these verbs have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different semantic valencies.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semasiology. The study of vocabulary starting specifically from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms rather than meanings. Opp. onomasiology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seme. See sememe.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semelfactive. (Verb, form of verb, etc.) used in reference to an event

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that happens just once: e.g. the past tense is semelfactive in He fell over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: yesterday, as compared with was falling in He was always falling over.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sememe. Term used by various scholars for a basic unit of meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus for Bloomfield a sememe was the meaning of a morpheme: e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the fishes the plural morpheme -s has as its meaning a sememe ‘more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semi-deponent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than one'. Also in European versions of *componential analysis, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the meaning of a lexical unit is a sememe (French ‘sémème' or its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equivalent) composed of semantic features or semes (French 'sèmes')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semi-deponent. Traditionally of a class of verbs in Latin whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms were like those of passives in perfect tenses but like those of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: actives in others. Hence 'partly *deponent'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semiology. See semiotics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semiotics. A general science of 'signs', of which, according to many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scholars in the 20th century, linguistics is part. Thus words and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphemes are 'signs', specifically *linguistic signs. So are traffic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lights, or gestures, or Christmas presents, or architectural features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: like a spire or pointed arch, or anything else that in the broadest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense 'has meaning'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The notion is due especially to Peirce and Saussure. 'Semiotics'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (originally ‘semiotic') is the term in the Peircean tradition for what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'sémiologie').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Saussure and the tradition following him call semiology (French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semi-productive. (Process, formation) permitting new combinations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of elements, but not with complete freedom. Used especially of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processes of *word-formation: e.g. it is possible, in principle, to form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new nouns like authoress from author or deaconess from deacon, but many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential forms, such as writeress or minist(e)ress, are not used and may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not be immediately clear or acceptable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
