layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Semitic. Family of languages which includes *Arabic and several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others of the Near East and Ethiopia, among them *Amharic,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Tigrinya, and *Hebrew. Others were important in antiquity,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially *Akkadian, *Aramaic, and *Phoenician. Divided into three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: main branches: East Semitic (= Akkadian); West Semitic (including

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Arabic and Hebrew); South Semitic (including Amharic and others in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea; also ancient and some modern languages in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Seen as a branch of *Afro-Asiatic (formerly 'Hamito-Semitic')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Semitic alphabets. Alphabets of a *consonantal type originally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed for *Semitic languages. Thus, among others, that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Arabic, subsequently adapted to non-Semitic languages, among them

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Persian and thence Urdu, with the spread of Islam.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The earliest alphabet for which we have evidence is that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Ugaritic, which used *cuneiform characters. Others are divided into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Semitic forms, attested mainly in the Arabian peninsula from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the early 1st millennium BC, and North Semitic, attested in Syria and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Palestine from the later 2nd millennium Bc. South Semitic is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: source of the alphabets now used for *Amharic and other languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Ethiopia; North Semitic for the remainder, and, from early in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1st millennium Bc, for the Greek alphabet and its Roman and other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: offshoots. The earliest form attested is that of *Phoenician; a related

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branch, called Canaanite, is found e.g. in early Hebrew inscriptions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and survives in the liturgical script of the Samaritans; all other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Semitic alphabets, including that of Arabic, derive from the form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed for *Aramaic at the beginning of the 1st millennium Bc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semivowel. A unit of sound which is phonetically like a *vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but whose place in syllable structure is characteristically that of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant: e.g. [j} in [jεs] (yes), phonetically a close front vowel, or [w)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in [wi:] (we), phonetically a close back vowel. Cf. glide.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense. 1. A meaning of a lexical unit distinguished, e.g. in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionary, from other meanings. Thus chair has one sense when it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used to refer to a piece of furniture and another when used to refer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to someone chairing a meeting. Cf. use for distinct meanings in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar. 2. The place of a lexical unit within the semantic system of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a language: e.g. that of chair is defined by the relations that distinguish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it from furniture, from armchair, from table, and so on. 3. The meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an expression as distinct from its *reference. Thus, in a famous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example of the philosopher G. Frege, the morning star and the evening

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: star have the same referent (the planet Venus) but differ in sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense relation. Any relation between lexical units within the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic system of a language; cf. sense (2). For types of sense relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: see antonymy; complementarity; converse terms; hyponymy;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: incompatibility; synonymy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensorimotor. (Activity, etc.) involving coordination of movement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with input from the senses. Especially with reference to the lowest and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: earliest of Piaget's proposed stages of cognitive development.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. Usually conceived, explicitly or implicitly, as the largest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit of grammar, or the largest unit over which a rule of grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can operate. E.g. in the sentence Come here! the order of come and here is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject to rule; but no rule governs a similar relation between it as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a whole and any other sentence that might precede or follow it in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Seen by many as a unit of the *language system. Thus Come here! is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence in English in the same sense that come is a word in English,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and one aim of a grammar of English is to delimit a set of well-formed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or *grammatical (2) combinations of words that includes it. Hence, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular, a widespread distinction between 'sentences' as abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entities or constructs, whose status is as units of the language system,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and *utterances or parts of utterances that correspond to or are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instances of them. E.g. in the utterance 'Come here! I love you', 'Come

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: here!' and 'I love you' instantiate, in the speech of a specific person at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a specific time, the sentences (conventionally represented in italics)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Come here! and I love you.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence adverb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also in two extended senses. 1. Of any unit structured like a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. E.g. in He said he was coming the clause he was coming is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: smaller sentence (German 'Nebensatz' or ‘subordinate sentence')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a larger. 2. Of analogous units in formal systems. Thus a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *formal 'language' is in mathematical terms any set of *strings, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a 'sentence' is correspondingly any member of such a set. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language' {ab, abc} has as its members the ‘sentences' ab and abc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. generative grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence adverb. An adverb whose semantic relation is to a whole

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence or clause, not just to a verb or verb phrase within it: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: obviously in Obviously, he didn't do it. Also called a 'sentential adverb'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as 'Who sent it?'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence fragment. Usually of a sentence reduced by *ellipsis to an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: incomplete form: e.g. My brother, uttered in answer to a question such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence grammar. A grammar that takes the sentence as its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: largest unit: i.e. one of the usual kind, as opposed e.g. to a 'discourse

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar' or a 'text grammar' in *textlinguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence meaning. Usually of meanings ascribed to *sentences in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the abstract, as opposed to those of *utterances. Cf. semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence stress. Any feature by which a syllable or sequence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syllables within a sentence is made more prominent than the rest.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus there is a difference in sentence stress between I left hER out, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emphasis on her, and I left her ouτ. Opp. word stress; cf. tonic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'sentence topic'. See topic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'sentence type'. Usually of statements, questions, etc. seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by *declarative, *interrogative, and other constructions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus He has gone represents one sentence type, Has he gone? another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence word. Bloomfield's term for a word which in itself

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completes a major sentence construction: e.g. Spanish salgo 'I am going

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: out' completes the construction of a subject with a predicate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentential. Of, related to, or consisting of, sentences. Sentential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coordination is *coordination of, or reduced from that of, sentences:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cf. phrasal coordination. A sentential relative clause is one in which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative pronoun relates to a predication rather than a noun phrase:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. which was rather silly in I said yes, which was rather silly. A sentential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complement is a *complement consisting of a sentence or clause:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. I was pleased as the complement of said in I said I was pleased. A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentential adverb is a *sentence adverb, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence. See order.

layout_dets.text: E.g. in He finished so he could be here tomorrow, the auxiliary could reflects

layout_dets.text: Sonoran. See Uto-Aztecan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sonorant. A speech sound in which air flows smoothly through the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vocal tract, without audible turbulence. Cf. resonant: both terms are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used variously, by different writers, either of vowels and of consonants

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which meet this definition, or of consonants only. See also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The feature [+ sonorant} is defined by Chomsky and Halle, *SPE, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of a sound 'produced with a vocal tract configuration in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spontaneous voicing is possible'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sonority.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sonority. The inherent loudness of a sound. E.g. if pitch, stress, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: length are equal, the vowel of barn is more sonorous than that of bean,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and either is more sonorous than the n and the b. In phonetic accounts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the syllable, the *nucleus (e.g. [a:| in barn) is represented as a peak of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called Wendish.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sorbian. West *Slavic language, spoken in Germany in the region of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cottbus and Bautzen, towards Poland and the Czech Republic. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sortal. Reflecting or indicating a sort or kind of entity. Thus a system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of noun classes might be described as sortal if, e.g. words for animals

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are of one class, words for plants in another, words for hard inanimate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects in a third, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sotho. *Bantu; the name is usually applied both to Northern Sotho,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the south and centre of the Transvaal in South Africa, and to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Southern Sotho, which has official status in Lesotho.
